Guideline Must Know: For hospitalized UGIB, employ a restrictive transfusion strategy—consider RBC transfusion at Hgb <7 g/dL in hemodynamically stable adults; reassess based on symptoms, ongoing bleeding, and ischemic heart disease risk

Guideline Must Know: Timing of endoscopy: after initial resuscitation, aim for upper endoscopy within 24 hours for admitted/observed UGIB; “crash to scope” is not automatically beneficial unless there is uncontrolled bleeding/instability requiring escalation
Guideline Must Know: Pre-endoscopy prokinetic can improve visualization when significant blood/clot suspected; erythromycin 250 mg IV 20–90 min pre-endoscopy is suggested in selected patients

Guideline Must Know: Post-endoscopic ulcer hemostasis requires high-dose acid suppression: high-dose PPI for 72 hours (continuous infusion or intermittent high-dose IV) followed by twice-daily oral PPI for 2 weeks to reduce rebleeding risk

Guideline Must Know: Endoscopic therapy is indicated for high-risk stigmata (active spurting/oozing, nonbleeding visible vessel); epinephrine injection alone is inadequate—use combination or definitive thermal/mechanical therapy; recurrent bleeding warrants repeat endoscopy and consider transcatheter embolization if endoscopy fails

Guideline Must Know: In confirmed H. pylori infection, treat and always confirm cure; when susceptibility is unknown, preferred first-line is optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days and avoid clarithromycin-based regimens unless susceptibility is documented; plan test-of-cure ≥4 weeks after therapy and after PPI washout per local practice

Night pitfalls: a “normal” initial hemoglobin can mask acute blood loss; trend vitals/mental status, check orthostatics if safe, and watch for rising BUN/creatinine ratio as a supportive clue; persistent tachycardia or narrow pulse pressure is a red flag even before labs drift

Medication pitfalls: stop NSAIDs immediately; assess aspirin indication—secondary prevention often needs early restart after hemostasis; coordinate DOAC/warfarin management with GI/ICU and avoid blanket reversal unless bleeding is life-threatening or intervention is imminent

Perforation presentation: sudden severe epigastric pain, rigid abdomen, shoulder pain, sepsis physiology, or free air; overnight priorities are NPO, broad-spectrum antibiotics, urgent CT/abd series, and immediate surgery consult—do not delay for “trial of PPI.”

Gastric outlet obstruction (from chronic ulcer/scarring): persistent nonbilious vomiting, early satiety, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; stabilize with IV fluids, electrolyte repletion, NG decompression if needed, and plan nonemergent endoscopic evaluation unless unstable

ICU/consult framing: call GI urgently for ongoing hematemesis/melena with instability or high transfusion needs; call surgery for peritonitis/perforation; involve cardiology when balancing antithrombotics in high-risk coronary disease

Confirm Before Proceed: irreversible actions include massive transfusion activation, anticoagulation reversal, and emergent intubation for endoscopy—document objective triggers (hemodynamics, lactate, airway risk) and coordinate multidisciplinary plan before pulling the lever

What can wait until daylight once stable: definitive NSAID risk mitigation (COX-2 vs avoidance), long-term PPI taper plan after ulcer healing, and outpatient malignancy evaluation for gastric ulcers (biopsy strategy per GI)

q.st: A 67-year-old man with osteoarthritis takes naproxen daily and presents with melena and lightheadedness. BP is 108/62 mmHg, HR 112/min. He is alert and has no abdominal tenderness. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, INR 1.0. Two large-bore IVs are placed and he receives 1 L of isotonic crystalloid with improved dizziness. What is the best next step in management overnight?
o: A. Transfuse 2 units packed RBCs immediately to target hemoglobin ≥10 g/dL
B. Arrange upper endoscopy within the next 24 hours after continued resuscitation and initiate high-dose IV PPI therapy
C. Start octreotide infusion and ceftriaxone for presumed variceal bleeding
D. Begin empiric H. pylori eradication therapy immediately without testing
E. Defer endoscopy until hemoglobin is ≥9 g/dL to reduce procedure risk
q.r: Guidelines recommend resuscitation followed by upper endoscopy within 24 hours for hospitalized UGIB and high-dose PPI therapy around endoscopic management of ulcer bleeding A restrictive transfusion strategy is favored in stable adults (often transfuse at Hgb <7 g/dL, individualized), so routine transfusion to ≥10 g/dL is not indicated here

q.st: A 74-year-old woman with prior myocardial infarction takes aspirin 81 mg daily for secondary prevention. She develops hematemesis and melena. After IV fluids, BP is 118/70 mmHg and HR is 96/min. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL. Endoscopy shows a bleeding duodenal ulcer that is successfully treated with endoscopic hemostasis. Which antiplatelet plan is most appropriate?
o: A. Stop aspirin indefinitely because it caused the bleeding ulcer
B. Hold aspirin for at least 30 days to prevent rebleeding
C. Resume aspirin as soon as possible after hemostasis because it is for secondary cardiovascular prevention
D. Switch aspirin to clopidogrel immediately and avoid PPI co-therapy
E. Start therapeutic heparin bridging while aspirin is held
q.r: A key pitfall is over-holding antiplatelet therapy in secondary prevention; guideline recommendations support continuing or early resumption of low-dose aspirin after hemostasis because cardiovascular risk is high and interruption should be minimized Co-therapy with acid suppression is commonly used after ulcer bleeding, and bridging anticoagulation is not indicated for aspirin interruption

m.q: In a hemodynamically stable adult with UGIB, at what hemoglobin threshold is RBC transfusion generally considered?
m.a: Consider transfusion at Hgb <7 g/dL using a restrictive strategy, individualized for symptoms and cardiovascular disease

m.q: What is the recommended timing target for inpatient endoscopy after presentation with UGIB?
m.a: Perform endoscopy within 24 hours after initial resuscitation for patients admitted or observed for UGIB

m.q: After endoscopic hemostasis of a high-risk bleeding ulcer, how long should high-dose PPI therapy be continued?
m.a: Continue high-dose PPI for 72 hours, then transition to twice-daily oral PPI for 2 weeks

m.q: For empiric first-line H. pylori treatment when susceptibility is unknown, what regimen duration is preferred?
m.a: Optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days is recommended as a preferred empiric first-line option

brief_overview: Tonight’s high-risk esophageal problems are not “routine GERD”: focus on airway/aspiration risk (drooling, inability to swallow saliva), perforation, bleeding, and obstructing dysphagia; stabilize first, then diagnose.

Guideline Must Know: For classic reflux symptoms without alarm features, the standard initial approach is an empiric PPI once daily 30–60 min before a meal for ~8 weeks; inpatient, this often means restarting/optimizing PPI timing rather than adding multiple agents.

Guideline Must Know: Alarm features (especially dysphagia, GI bleeding, weight loss) warrant endoscopy as first test rather than empiric escalation; if these appear overnight, keep NPO after midnight, place consult early, and avoid delaying with non-diagnostic barium studies.

Separate “what must happen now” vs “what can wait”: now = airway/aspiration evaluation, hemodynamic stabilization, sepsis screen if perforation suspected, and urgent consults for obstruction/bleeding; can wait = lifestyle counseling, outpatient reflux testing, and long-term cancer prevention discussions.

Refractory “GERD” on the floor often isn’t GERD: think pill esophagitis (doxycycline, bisphosphonates, KCl), infectious esophagitis (immunosuppression), EoE, achalasia, or malignancy; new progressive dysphagia is a red flag, especially solids → liquids.

Esophageal food impaction: key pivot is whether the patient can manage secretions; inability to swallow saliva, persistent drooling, or respiratory symptoms = emergent endoscopy pathway, keep NPO, avoid giving large volumes by mouth, and prepare for airway management.

Guideline Must Know: ASGE guidance prioritizes urgent endoscopic removal for high-risk esophageal impactions (airway risk, complete obstruction, sharp objects, batteries) and recommends structured evaluation rather than “watchful waiting” when obstruction is complete.

Suspected perforation (Boerhaave, post-procedure): treat as time-critical sepsis source; immediate NPO + broad IV antibiotics + early surgery consult; obtain CT chest/abdomen (often with water-soluble oral contrast if tolerated) and avoid anything that increases intraluminal pressure.
GERD mimics during night float: cardiac ischemia, PE, aortic pathology, pancreatitis; for chest pain, do not anchor on reflux until life-threatening causes are reasonably excluded.

Guideline Must Know: Achalasia is suggested by dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, weight loss, or “GERD” unresponsive to acid suppression; definitive diagnosis is by high-resolution manometry, but inpatient role is to recognize pattern, keep aspiration precautions, and arrange GI workup.

Guideline Must Know: Treatment selection for achalasia depends on subtype; PD, LHM, and POEM are effective options for many patients, with POEM favored for type III in guidelines—overnight, the key is early recognition and avoiding inappropriate escalation of acid suppression alone.

Guideline Must Know: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a common cause of recurrent food impaction and dysphagia; guideline-based therapy includes PPI, swallowed topical steroids, elimination diets, and dilation for fibrostenosis, but inpatient action is mainly obstruction management and ensuring biopsy/diagnostic follow-up.

Infectious esophagitis clues: severe odynophagia, immunosuppression, oral thrush (candida), deep chest pain; stabilize pain control, hydration, and consult GI if severe/bleeding/obstructing; avoid empiric steroids unless clear indication.

Bleeding from severe reflux esophagitis or ulcer: treat as UGIB—resuscitate, correct shock, hold anticoagulants when safe, and coordinate urgent endoscopy timing; give IV PPI for suspected high-risk lesions while awaiting GI plan.

Inpatient medication strategy: if aspiration risk or strict NPO, use IV PPI (e.g., pantoprazole) and IV antiemetics; if able to take PO, prioritize correct timing and avoid duplicative acid suppression unless there is a clear nocturnal breakthrough plan.

Pitfalls: missing perforation after vomiting/endoscopy; giving oral meds/food to a complete obstruction; assuming all dysphagia is “GERD”; and delaying escalation when objective triggers appear (new oxygen need, rising lactate, fever, hypotension, mediastinal air).

q.st: A 58-year-old man is admitted for COPD exacerbation. Overnight he reports burning retrosternal discomfort and sour taste that worsen after meals and when lying flat. He denies dysphagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. Vitals are stable, and his cardiac workup earlier in the day was negative. Which is the best initial management?
o: A. Start a proton pump inhibitor once daily 30–60 minutes before breakfast for 8 weeks
B. Start sucralfate scheduled four times daily and stop all acid suppression
C. Order a barium swallow as the first diagnostic test
D. Start baclofen nightly for presumed reflux-related symptoms
E. Order urgent upper endoscopy tonight
q.r: For classic reflux symptoms without alarm features, guidelines recommend an empiric 8-week trial of a once-daily PPI taken 30–60 minutes before a meal as the initial step. q.st: A 66-year-old woman on alendronate is admitted for cellulitis. D. Place a nasogastric tube for decompression and medication delivery
E. Start high-dose oral steroids immediately

m.a: When there is dysphagia or other alarm symptoms such as GI bleeding or weight loss.

m.q: How should a PPI be timed for best symptom control when given orally?
m.a: 30–60 minutes before a meal, typically before breakfast.

If infection/alternate acute abdomen possible (fever, leukocytosis, peritonitis): broaden differential and evaluate now (stool studies/CT as indicated); do not anchor on “celiac flare.”

Confirm Before Proceed: avoid committing the patient to a lifelong gluten-free diet label before diagnostic confirmation unless clinically necessary (e.g., unstable malabsorption requiring immediate nutrition changes).
brief_overview: Night-float framing: inpatient “celiac disease” issues are usually (1) undiagnosed malabsorption presenting as diarrhea/weight loss/anemia, (2) diagnosed celiac with persistent symptoms from gluten exposure or another diagnosis, or (3) complications (electrolyte derangements, severe anemia, bone/mineral issues, rare celiac crisis).

Guideline Must Know: Initial testing in adults should be done while the patient is on a gluten-containing diet; gluten restriction before testing lowers sensitivity of both serology and biopsy and is discouraged unless the situation demands immediate dietary change.

Guideline Must Know: First-line serology is tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) plus total IgA to detect IgA deficiency; if IgA deficient, use tTG-IgG and/or deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) IgG rather than relying on IgA-based tests.

Guideline Must Know: Diagnostic confirmation in most adults requires EGD with multiple duodenal biopsies (including bulb and distal duodenum) because disease can be patchy; don’t assume a single normal-appearing biopsy rules it out.

Guideline Must Know: If clinical suspicion is high with negative serology (e.g., classic malabsorption, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis), proceed to EGD/biopsies for possible seronegative celiac disease or alternative enteropathy.

Guideline Must Know: If the patient is already on a gluten-free diet and needs diagnosis clarified, consider HLA-DQ2/DQ8: a negative result makes celiac disease very unlikely; a positive result is not diagnostic and may prompt a supervised gluten challenge planning with GI.

Guideline Must Know: Management cornerstone is strict gluten-free diet with dietitian involvement; inpatient role is to ensure safe nutrition orders and avoid iatrogenic gluten exposure in meds/supplements when feasible, while coordinating outpatient follow-up.

Now (what must happen tonight): stabilize volume/electrolytes; evaluate for competing dangerous diagnoses (sepsis, C. difficile, GI bleed, obstruction, pancreatitis); document stool frequency/volume, intake, and objective weight trends; review meds that worsen diarrhea (metformin, laxatives, antibiotics, magnesium supplements).

Now (diagnostic triage): if undiagnosed and stable, order celiac serologies and arrange GI follow-up for biopsy; if already admitted for another reason and suspicion is high, place a non-urgent GI consult for inpatient EGD decision-making (especially if anemia, severe symptoms, or need to clarify diagnosis before discharge).

Pitfall: starting a strict gluten-free diet immediately in a stable, undiagnosed patient can delay definitive diagnosis because serology and histology may normalize; if symptoms are severe and diet must change, document the reason and coordinate a plan for future diagnostic confirmation.

Can wait (unless unstable): micronutrient evaluation and replacement planning (iron studies, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, zinc), bone health counseling, and long-term complication screening; start replacement inpatient if clearly deficient or symptomatic (e.g., hypocalcemia, severe iron deficiency).

Nonresponsive symptoms in known celiac disease are commonly due to ongoing gluten exposure; on nights, focus on ruling out urgent mimics/complications and initiating a systematic plan: repeat serology, diet review, and consider other causes (microscopic colitis, pancreatic insufficiency, IBS, lactose intolerance, medication-related diarrhea).

Red flags for complications: new severe abdominal pain, weight loss despite reported adherence, GI bleeding, fevers, night sweats, obstructive symptoms, or unexplained hypoalbuminemia—consider malignancy (e.g., enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma) or refractory disease; involve GI early.

Rare but high-risk: “celiac crisis” (profuse diarrhea, dehydration, metabolic derangements, hypoproteinemia) may require ICU-level monitoring, aggressive repletion, and specialist input; consider concomitant infection and adrenal insufficiency when hypotension is disproportionate.

Dermatitis herpetiformis clue: intensely pruritic grouped vesicles (elbows/knees/buttocks/scalp) strongly supports gluten-sensitive disease; symptomatic rash control (often dapsone) is typically specialist-managed—on nights, focus on symptom relief, exclude infection, and arrange dermatology/GI follow-up.

Discharge priorities: ensure a clear diagnostic plan (serology results pending, biopsy plan if needed), dietitian referral, and follow-up for anemia/micronutrients; document whether patient was consuming gluten during testing and whether gluten restriction was started inpatient.

q.st: A 34-year-old hospitalized patient reports 6 months of diarrhea, bloating, and unintentional weight loss. Labs show microcytic anemia and mildly elevated aminotransferases. They are eating a normal diet that includes wheat. You suspect celiac disease and want the best initial diagnostic test strategy tonight.
o: A. Start a strict gluten-free diet now and recheck symptoms in 2 weeks
B. Order tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA
C. Order HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping only
D. Order anti-saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)
E. Order stool calprotectin as the primary diagnostic test
q.r: In adults on a gluten-containing diet, the recommended first-line evaluation is tTG-IgA with total IgA to screen and identify IgA deficiency that would invalidate IgA-only testing. Most adults then require confirmatory EGD with duodenal biopsies if serology is positive or suspicion remains high. HLA testing is mainly useful to rule out celiac disease when patients are already gluten-free, not as an initial standalone test.

q.st: A 52-year-old patient with chronic diarrhea and iron-deficiency anemia started a gluten-free diet 3 months ago on their own and reports partial improvement. They are now admitted for syncope and found to have orthostatic hypotension but are otherwise stable. You need to clarify whether they truly have celiac disease.
o: A. Order tissue transglutaminase IgA only
B. Order HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping
C. Start oral budesonide for presumed refractory celiac disease
D. Diagnose celiac disease based on symptom improvement alone and continue gluten avoidance
E. Order duodenal biopsies immediately without considering diet status
q.r: When a patient has already reduced or eliminated gluten, serology and biopsy may normalize and become less reliable for diagnosis; in this setting, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 negativity effectively rules out celiac disease, while positivity is non-diagnostic and may lead to a supervised gluten challenge plan with GI. The pitfall is assuming symptom improvement on a gluten-free diet confirms the diagnosis. What changed the decision here?

m.q: For best diagnostic accuracy, should celiac serology and biopsy be performed while the patient is eating gluten?
m.a: Yes. Gluten restriction before testing can reduce the sensitivity of both serology and histology.

m.q: Which two labs should be ordered together as first-line celiac screening in most adults?
m.a: Tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA.

m.q: In suspected celiac disease with IgA deficiency, which antibody class is preferred?
m.a: IgG-based testing (tTG-IgG and/or DGP-IgG).

m.q: What does a negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 test imply in a patient already on a gluten-free diet?
m.a: It makes celiac disease very unlikely.

Place contact enteric precautions now for new-onset inpatient diarrhea until infectious etiologies (esp. C. difficile) addressed; stop laxatives and high-risk meds
Check bedside red flags: SBP <90, HR ≥120, fever ≥38.5°C, severe abdominal pain, bloody stool, AMS, oliguria, lactate ≥2 mmol/L → escalate evaluation and consider ICU.

If suspected severe/fulminant CDI (hypotension, ileus, megacolon): start therapy promptly while testing; Confirm Before Proceed: avoid antimotility agents in suspected inflammatory diarrhea/CDI
brief_overview: Acute diarrhea in inpatients is often medication- or tube feed–related, but overnight you must first rule out dangerous infectious/inflammatory causes: C. difficile, invasive bacterial colitis, ischemic colitis, and sepsis; treat dehydration and hemodynamic instability immediately, then refine etiology

Guideline Must Know: Evaluate all patients for dehydration and severity (orthostasis, dry mucosa, oliguria, AKI); severe dehydration or sepsis physiology warrants IV rehydration rather than oral-only replacement.

Now: stop obvious iatrogenic drivers (laxatives, stool softeners, magnesium-containing antacids, metformin, new antibiotics, tube feed osmolarity changes) and quantify stool output; document # unformed stools/24 h and presence of blood/mucus because it drives testing and antimotility safety.

Guideline Must Know: Send stool testing when diarrhea is accompanied by fever, bloody or mucoid stools, severe cramping/tenderness, or signs of sepsis; recommended targets include Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile, and STEC (Shiga toxin).

Guideline Must Know: When STEC is possible (bloody diarrhea, severe cramps, outbreak/food exposure), ensure testing detects Shiga toxin and distinguishes E. coli O157:H7 from non-O157 STEC; avoid empiric antibiotics if STEC suspected unless compelling sepsis indications.

Guideline Must Know: In hospitalized patients, prioritize C. difficile when diarrhea is new/unexplained and especially after antibiotic exposure; test only when symptomatic (e.g., ≥3 unformed stools in 24 h) and off laxatives when feasible to reduce false positives from colonization.

Guideline Must Know: IDSA/SHEA 2021 focused update: for an initial CDI episode, fidaxomicin is suggested over vancomycin when feasible, but vancomycin remains acceptable; choose based on severity, resources, and stewardship

Guideline Must Know: Fulminant CDI (hypotension/shock, ileus, megacolon) requires aggressive resuscitation plus vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG q6h and consider metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h; add rectal vancomycin if ileus prevents adequate luminal delivery

Now: decide if empiric antibiotics are warranted—most acute watery diarrhea is self-limited; empiric therapy is generally reserved for sepsis, severe traveler-associated disease, or high-risk hosts, and should be narrowed once testing returns

Guideline Must Know: Do not give antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide) when bloody diarrhea, high fever, suspected C. difficile, suspected toxic megacolon, or significant abdominal tenderness—risk of worsening invasive disease/ileus; symptomatic agents are safer for uncomplicated watery diarrhea

Now: if abdominal exam suggests peritonitis, severe focal tenderness, or concern for ischemic colitis/megacolon, obtain urgent imaging (CT A/P with IV contrast if renal function allows) and consult surgery/GI early; do not anchor on “gastroenteritis” in an older inpatient with pain out of proportion.

Now: correct complications of volume/electrolyte losses—metabolic acidosis (low HCO₃⁻), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and prerenal AKI; replete electrolytes proactively if ongoing stool losses and monitor QT-risk meds overnight.

Later: review antimicrobials and stewardship—stop unnecessary antibiotics driving diarrhea/CDI risk, and if antibiotics are required for another indication, document the rationale and planned duration to reduce recurrence risk.

Later: if symptoms persist >7 days or are moderate-to-severe, broaden evaluation (culture-independent stool panels, ova/parasite testing when epidemiologically indicated, medication review, thyroid/adrenal considerations) and plan daytime follow-up for chronic/persistent workup

Pitfalls: false-positive C. difficile NAAT in colonized patients (treat the patient, not the PCR); missing early fulminant CDI (rising WBC/Cr, ileus); giving loperamide in inflammatory diarrhea; and failing to isolate promptly, causing unit outbreaks

Severe inflammatory diarrhea: gross blood, Hgb drop, or escalating abdominal pain/tenderness requiring urgent imaging/endoscopic planning.
Worsening organ dysfunction: rising creatinine/oliguria, severe electrolyte derangements (e.g., K⁺ <3.0 mmol/L despite repletion), or new arrhythmia/QT prolongation.

q.st: A 68-year-old man is hospitalized for pneumonia and has received ceftriaxone and azithromycin for 5 days. Overnight he develops 6 watery bowel movements, abdominal cramping, and a temperature of 38.6°C. Vitals: BP 104/62 mmHg, HR 112/min. Labs: WBC 18,500/µL, creatinine increased from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL. He has no peritoneal signs. What is the best next step in management?
o: A. Give loperamide and observe because most inpatient diarrhea is self-limited
B. Start oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily and place contact enteric precautions while sending C. difficile testing
C. Start oral ciprofloxacin for empiric bacterial gastroenteritis and send a stool culture
D. Order colonoscopy urgently to confirm pseudomembranes before any treatment
E. Send stool ova and parasite examination and defer therapy until results return
q.r: This patient has high suspicion for CDI with systemic features and renal dysfunction; prompt isolation and empiric therapy are appropriate while diagnostic testing is sent. IDSA/SHEA recommend fidaxomicin when feasible for initial CDI, but vancomycin remains an acceptable alternative, and early treatment is critical when severity features are present. Antimotility therapy is inappropriate when inflammatory infectious diarrhea/CDI is suspected

q.st: A 34-year-old woman is admitted for IV antibiotics for cellulitis. Overnight she develops sudden severe crampy abdominal pain and multiple episodes of bloody diarrhea after eating a hamburger brought from home earlier that day. Vitals: T 38.2°C, BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 105/min. Exam shows diffuse tenderness without guarding. What is the best next step?
o: A. Start empiric azithromycin immediately and give loperamide for symptom control
B. Send stool testing for Shiga toxin–producing organisms and provide supportive care without antibiotics or antimotility agents
C. Start high-dose oral vancomycin because bloody diarrhea strongly suggests C. difficile infection
D. Administer prednisone for presumed inflammatory bowel disease flare
E. Give bismuth subsalicylate and discharge because vitals are stable
q.r: Bloody diarrhea with severe cramps after beef exposure raises concern for STEC; guidelines emphasize testing that detects Shiga toxin and caution against routine empiric antibiotics in suspected STEC due to potential harm (pitfall: worsening risk of HUS). Supportive care with careful monitoring is preferred while diagnostics are obtained. Avoid antimotility agents in inflammatory diarrhea. What changed the decision here?

m.q: What stool frequency criterion supports testing for symptomatic C. difficile in adults?
m.a: ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours in a patient with compatible symptoms and no clear alternate cause.

m.q: In which scenario should you avoid loperamide overnight?
m.a: When there is bloody diarrhea, high fever, suspected C. difficile, or significant abdominal tenderness suggesting inflammatory colitis

m.q: Which stool features mandate bacterial pathogen testing per IDSA infectious diarrhea guidance?
m.a: Diarrhea with fever, bloody/mucoid stools, severe abdominal cramping/tenderness, or signs of sepsis.

m.q: What is the first-line enteric isolation action for suspected infectious inpatient diarrhea?
m.a: Place contact enteric precautions immediately while evaluation is underway

Check immediate danger labs: BMP + Mg²⁺ + phosphate, VBG/ABG if ill; replete aggressively for K⁺ <3.0 mmol/L or Mg²⁺ <1.6 mg/dL and place on telemetry if significant derangements/arrhythmia risk.
If inpatient/antibiotic exposure or ≥3 unformed stools/24 h: send C. difficile testing and institute contact precautions; avoid antimotility agents if severe/systemic illness

Evaluate for red flags requiring escalation now: fever, bloody stool, severe abdominal pain/peritonitis, AKI/oliguria, rising lactate, or concern for toxic megacolon; stop laxatives and suspect meds (Mg, metformin, PPIs/NSAIDs)
Confirm Before Proceed: Do not give loperamide/opioids until you have excluded C. difficile, invasive bacterial diarrhea, ileus, or suspected megacolon/obstruction (risk of worsening outcomes)
brief_overview: Define the inpatient problem: chronic diarrhea is ≥4 weeks of loose stools; on night float, prioritize stabilizing volume/electrolytes, identifying infectious/systemic causes, and preventing iatrogenic worsening (laxatives, tube feeds, antibiotics, metformin, magnesium, sorbitol)

First fork is severity and “alarm” physiology: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65, HR ≥120, new confusion, lactate ≥2 mmol/L, Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL/48 h, K⁺ <2.5 or >6.0 mmol/L, severe abdominal tenderness/guarding, or ongoing GI bleeding = treat as unstable and escalate early (ICU/consult)

What must happen now: quantify output (stools/24 h, nocturnal stools, ostomy output), start strict I/Os, check orthostatics, and order targeted labs: CBC, CMP, Mg²⁺, phosphate, consider TSH and morning cortisol if chronic unexplained watery diarrhea with weight loss/hypotension

Infectious rule-out is common in hospitalized adults even with “chronic” symptoms: if ≥3 unformed stools/24 h with recent antibiotics/healthcare exposure, test for C. difficile and stop inciting antibiotics when feasible; consider stool PCR/culture only when fever, bloody stool, severe pain, sepsis signs, or immunocompromise

Guideline Must Know: For watery diarrhea ≥4 weeks without alarm features, AGA recommends targeted labs rather than exhaustive testing; use fecal calprotectin or fecal lactoferrin to screen for inflammatory conditions (IBD) when appropriate

Guideline Must Know: AGA recommends testing for Giardia in adults with chronic watery diarrhea because it is common and readily treatable; don’t miss it in patients with daycare exposure, contaminated water risk, or unexplained persistent watery stools
Guideline Must Know: AGA suggests against ESR/CRP alone as screening for IBD in chronic watery diarrhea pathways; prefer stool inflammatory markers when the clinical question is “IBD vs functional.”

Guideline Must Know: AGA recommends celiac testing with tTG-IgA plus total IgA (add an IgG-based assay if IgA deficient) in chronic diarrhea/IBS-D-like presentations; ensure the patient is ingesting gluten if evaluating for new diagnosis

Guideline Must Know: AGA suggests evaluating for bile acid diarrhea in chronic watery diarrhea (especially post-cholecystectomy/ileal disease); inpatient “practical” approach when formal testing unavailable is a time-limited trial of a bile acid sequestrant once infection excluded

Guideline Must Know: IDSA emphasizes stool testing for bacterial pathogens when diarrhea is accompanied by fever, bloody/mucoid stools, severe abdominal cramping/tenderness, or sepsis signs; otherwise avoid broad stool workups that drive false positives and downstream harm.

Categorize stool phenotype to avoid shotgun orders: watery (secretory/osmotic), fatty (malabsorption), inflammatory (blood, high calprotectin), and medication-related; nocturnal watery diarrhea and large-volume output suggest secretory causes (e.g., bile acid diarrhea, microscopic colitis, endocrine) more than functional etiologies

Microscopic colitis is a classic “overnight miss”: chronic watery diarrhea (often nocturnal) with a grossly normal colon; review triggers (PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs) and remember diagnosis requires colonic biopsies; first-line therapy for symptomatic disease is budesonide when confirmed or strongly suspected with GI input

C. difficile can masquerade as chronic diarrhea (especially with intermittent antibiotics/PPIs): use guideline-based therapy for confirmed cases; fidaxomicin is preferred when available, with oral vancomycin an acceptable alternative for initial episodes per IDSA/SHEA focused update.

What can usually wait until daytime: breath tests for carbohydrate malabsorption/SIBO, advanced malabsorption panels, and colonoscopy scheduling decisions when the patient is stable; what should not wait is stopping offending agents, correcting volume/electrolytes, and placing isolation if infectious risk

Pitfalls: giving antimotility agents before excluding C. difficile/invasive infection, missing microscopic colitis due to “normal colonoscopy,” and overlooking iatrogenic diarrhea from tube feeds, sorbitol-containing meds, Mg supplements, or laxative protocols that were never discontinued

When to call GI urgently: suspected severe IBD flare, persistent high-output diarrhea with worsening AKI, need for inpatient colonoscopy/biopsies, concern for ischemic colitis/toxic megacolon, or refractory symptoms despite stopping offenders and addressing infection
icu_consult_triggers: MAP <65 mmHg after ≥2 L isotonic fluids (or fluid-limited patient with ongoing hypoperfusion), lactate ≥2 mmol/L, or need for vasopressors.
Severe electrolyte/acid-base derangements: K⁺ <2.5 or >6.0 mmol/L, symptomatic hypomagnesemia, severe metabolic acidosis, or arrhythmia/ECG changes.
Suspected fulminant colitis/toxic megacolon: severe abdominal pain/distension, ileus, peritonitis, rising WBC/creatinine, or systemic toxicity (especially with possible C. difficile)
Overt GI bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or concern for ischemic colitis (pain out of proportion, bloody diarrhea with vascular risk).
Immunocompromised host with persistent diarrhea plus fever, sepsis physiology, or inability to maintain hydration/renal function on the floor.

q.st: A 46-year-old man is admitted for evaluation of 6 weeks of nonbloody, watery diarrhea (6–8 stools/day) with mild cramping. He is immunocompetent and has no weight loss, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, recent travel, or family history of inflammatory bowel disease. Vital signs are stable. Basic metabolic panel and complete blood count are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
o: A. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
B. Stool ova and parasite examination (multiple specimens)
C. Stool test for Giardia
D. Serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)
E. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics
q.r: AGA guidance for adults with chronic watery diarrhea without alarm features recommends targeted testing and specifically recommends testing for Giardia, a common, treatable cause Routine broad ova/parasite testing without high-risk travel is not recommended, and ESR/CRP or autoimmune serologies are not appropriate screening tests for this presentation

q.st: A 72-year-old woman hospitalized for atrial fibrillation is noted to have 3 months of chronic watery diarrhea, including nocturnal episodes. She takes a proton pump inhibitor and ibuprofen daily. She has no fever or blood in stool. A colonoscopy performed 2 weeks ago showed normal-appearing mucosa throughout. Current labs show normal hemoglobin and albumin. Which is the best next step to establish the diagnosis?
o: A. Reassure her that a normal colonoscopy rules out colitis
B. Start loperamide immediately as first-line therapy
C. Obtain random colonic biopsies to evaluate for microscopic colitis
D. Order ESR and CRP to exclude inflammatory bowel disease
E. Start empiric oral vancomycin for presumed C. difficile
q.r: The pitfall is assuming a normal-appearing colon excludes microscopic colitis; diagnosis requires colonic biopsies despite normal endoscopic appearance Medication exposures such as PPIs/NSAIDs increase suspicion, and confirming the diagnosis guides appropriate therapy (often budesonide)

m.q: What duration defines chronic diarrhea in adults?
m.a: ≥4 weeks of loose or watery stools

m.q: In an immunocompetent adult with chronic watery diarrhea and no alarm features, which single stool pathogen test is specifically recommended?
m.a: Giardia testing

m.q: What stool inflammatory markers are suggested to screen for inflammatory conditions such as IBD in chronic watery diarrhea pathways?
m.a: Fecal calprotectin or fecal lactoferrin

m.q: What is the preferred target population for C. difficile testing in adults?
m.a: Adults with ≥3 new, unexplained unformed stools in 24 hours.

Stop hepatotoxins and review meds now: acetaminophen, statins, isoniazid, valproate, amiodarone, herbals; hold non-essential anticoagulants if active bleeding/coagulopathy.
If active GI bleed or hemodynamic instability in cirrhosis: resuscitate, type & screen, start GI bleed pathway (octreotide + ceftriaxone if variceal suspected), and call GI urgently.

Guideline Must Know: For HBV screening in adults, use the triple panel: HBsAg + anti-HBs + total anti-HBc at least once in adults ≥18 years (and in pregnancy each pregnancy). This matters inpatient because it prevents missed chronic HBV before steroids/chemo and identifies susceptibility for vaccination.

Guideline Must Know: For HCV, confirm active infection with HCV RNA (not antibody alone). HCV antibody positive can reflect resolved infection; RNA drives counseling, infection control, and outpatient cure plans.

When AST/ALT are >1000 IU/L, do not anchor on “viral hepatitis” first: prioritize ischemic hepatitis/shock liver, acetaminophen toxicity, and acute biliary obstruction; order acetaminophen level, lactate, INR, RUQ ultrasound ± Doppler, and review hypotension episodes.

Guideline Must Know: HBV reactivation is a high-risk inpatient pitfall: any patient who is HBsAg positive OR anti-HBc positive (even if HBsAg negative) can reactivate with immunosuppression; the risk is highest with anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab/obinutuzumab), hematopoietic stem-cell transplant, and intensive combination chemo.

Guideline Must Know: If high-risk immunosuppression is imminent and HBV status is positive (HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+), start prophylactic antiviral therapy rather than “monitoring only.” Preferred agents are high-barrier nucleos(t)ide analogs: entecavir or tenofovir; coordinate with hepatology/ID early because timing matters before the first immunosuppressive dose.

Practical overnight triage for a new positive HBV test: check HBsAg, anti-HBc (IgM if available), anti-HBs, and if HBsAg positive order HBV DNA plus HBeAg/anti-HBe; assess severity with INR, bilirubin, platelets, and symptoms. Isolated anti-HBc (HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative) can represent remote infection, false positive, or occult HBV—do not dismiss it if immunosuppression is planned.

Guideline Must Know: For inpatient HCV “found incidentally,” do not start DAAs overnight unless a coordinated plan exists; instead confirm HCV RNA, assess fibrosis noninvasively (e.g., FIB-4) and decompensation status, and ensure drug–drug interaction review—these are core steps in AASLD/IDSA HCV guidance.

If planning HCV treatment (even as outpatient), always check HBV first because DAAs can be associated with HBV reactivation in susceptible patients; order HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs up front to avoid delays and missed prophylaxis.

Guideline Must Know: In suspected acute severe viral hepatitis or flare, severity is about synthetic function, not just transaminases: INR, bilirubin, encephalopathy, and glucose determine disposition; worsening INR/encephalopathy should trigger ICU-level monitoring and hepatology involvement.

What must happen now vs what can wait: now—rule out acute liver failure, identify acetaminophen/ischemic causes, evaluate for biliary obstruction, determine need for ICU/consults, and address infection control/exposure questions; can wait—full staging, vaccination counseling, and definitive antiviral cure planning once stable.

Night shift pitfalls: mislabeling “HCV positive” based on antibody alone; forgetting HBV prophylaxis before rituximab or prolonged high-dose steroids; attributing AST/ALT >1000 to “hepatitis” without checking acetaminophen; overcorrecting coagulopathy without bleeding; giving sedatives in evolving encephalopathy.

Consult-smart language: “Concern for HBV reactivation in anti-HBc positive patient receiving rituximab tomorrow” or “Possible acute liver failure: INR 2.1 + new confusion” gets faster escalation than “hepatitis flare.”

Infection prevention basics for the floor: standard precautions; notify occupational health for needlestick or mucosal exposure; document source-patient HBV/HCV/HIV status and initial labs so follow-up doesn’t fall through overnight.
icu_consult_triggers: INR ≥1.5 with any encephalopathy or rapidly rising INR/bilirubin over hours.
Persistent hypoglycemia, escalating lactate, or hemodynamic instability suggesting ischemic hepatitis/shock.

New severe jaundice with fever, hypotension, or RUQ pain concerning for cholangitis/obstructive process requiring urgent imaging and intervention.

q.st: A 62-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is admitted overnight to start rituximab-based chemotherapy in the morning. Pre-chemotherapy labs show HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, and total anti-HBc positive. ALT is 34 IU/L and INR is 1.0. He has no known liver disease. What is the best next step tonight to reduce his risk of hepatitis-related complications during treatment?
o: A. Begin entecavir prophylaxis now and continue through and after immunosuppression per protocol
B. No action; repeat liver enzymes weekly during chemotherapy
C. Administer hepatitis B vaccine now and proceed with chemotherapy without antivirals
D. Start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir to prevent viral hepatitis flares
E. Give hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) immediately before rituximab infusion
q.r: Anti-HBc positivity indicates prior HBV exposure and risk for HBV reactivation with high-risk immunosuppression such as anti-CD20 therapy; guidelines favor prophylactic antiviral therapy over monitoring alone in this setting. Entecavir (or tenofovir) has a high barrier to resistance and is appropriate to start before the first rituximab dose. Vaccination does not prevent reactivation, DAAs treat HCV not HBV, and HBIG is not the standard prophylaxis strategy for this indication.

q.st: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is admitted for hypoxemic respiratory failure from presumed organizing pneumonia. The team plans to start prednisone 60 mg daily tonight with a slow taper over months. Her HBV tests return: HBsAg positive, anti-HBs negative, total anti-HBc positive. ALT is 78 IU/L and HBV DNA is pending. What is the best next step tonight?
o: A. Start tenofovir or entecavir now for HBV treatment/prophylaxis while steroids begin
B. Delay steroids until HBV DNA results return
C. Give hepatitis B vaccine now and reassess in 1 month
D. Start ribavirin to prevent hepatitis flare during steroids
E. Monitor ALT weekly; start antivirals only if ALT rises above 200 IU/L
q.r: HBsAg positivity indicates chronic HBV infection, and high-dose prolonged steroids can precipitate severe HBV reactivation/flares; starting a high-barrier antiviral (tenofovir or entecavir) promptly is recommended when significant immunosuppression is initiated. The pitfall is “waiting for HBV DNA” despite a clear high-risk trigger and positive HBsAg. Vaccination and ribavirin are inappropriate here, and monitoring alone risks preventable hepatic injury.

m.q: A patient is HCV antibody positive on admission labs. What single test confirms active infection?
m.a: Quantitative HCV RNA confirms active infection; antibody alone does not.

m.q: Which 3 tests make up the HBV “triple panel” screening?
m.a: HBsAg, anti-HBs, and total anti-HBc.

m.q: In suspected acute liver failure, what lab + clinical finding defines the syndrome that mandates urgent escalation?
m.a: INR ≥1.5 plus any encephalopathy in a patient without known cirrhosis.

m.q: Name one immunosuppressive therapy that is considered high risk for HBV reactivation.
m.a: Anti-CD20 therapy (e.g., rituximab) is high risk.

panic_card: Treat as surgical emergency: large-bore IV x2, NPO, oxygen to SpO₂ ≥92% (or baseline goal), place on monitor, and start crystalloid bolus 500–1000 mL if hypotensive while reassessing for overload.
STAT imaging: order CTA abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast NOW (do not delay for creatinine if life-threatening concern) and call general surgery + vascular surgery/IR immediately if high suspicion.
Start empiric infection control: give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour (gut translocation risk) and draw lactate, CBC, CMP, VBG/ABG.

Start anticoagulation if no major contraindication: unfractionated heparin bolus 80 units/kg IV then infusion 18 units/kg/h titrate to therapeutic aPTT/anti-Xa; hold only for active life-threatening bleeding.
Red flags = OR/ICU: peritonitis, persistent lactate rise, pH <7.30, pressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg, or worsening shock/mental status despite resuscitation.
brief_overview: Think “pain out of proportion” plus risk factors: atrial fibrillation/recent MI (embolus), diffuse atherosclerosis (thrombosis), shock/pressors (non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia, NOMI), hypercoagulable states/cancer/portal HTN (mesenteric venous thrombosis, MVT); early exam may be benign until infarction occurs.

What must happen now: stabilize perfusion and oxygenation, get CTA immediately, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, and involve surgery + vascular/IR early; time lost equals bowel lost and mortality rises when diagnosis/treatment are delayed.

Guideline Must Know: In suspected acute mesenteric ischemia, CTA should be performed without delay as the first-line diagnostic test; plain abdominal radiographs are not recommended to “rule it out,” and labs alone cannot exclude ischemia.

Guideline Must Know: Start resuscitation as soon as AMI is suspected: restore intravascular volume, correct electrolytes/acid-base issues, and decompress stomach if vomiting/ileus; aim for MAP ≥65 mmHg with careful reassessment (over-resuscitation can worsen gut edema/compartment physiology).
Guideline Must Know: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately (risk of bacterial translocation/sepsis once ischemia occurs), even before definitive proof if clinical suspicion is high.

Guideline Must Know: Unless contraindicated, initiate systemic anticoagulation with IV unfractionated heparin early in AMI (especially arterial embolus/thrombosis and MVT); UFH is preferred on nights because it is rapidly titratable and reversible.

Guideline Must Know: If there is overt peritonitis (rebound/guarding/rigidity), do not wait for “perfect” labs or serial exams: urgent laparotomy/laparoscopy for source control, bowel viability assessment, and resection of necrotic bowel is indicated.

Guideline Must Know: For arterial occlusion (embolus or thrombosis) and when expertise is available, endovascular revascularization is preferred (e.g., embolectomy/thrombectomy, angioplasty/stenting), with open surgery reserved for select cases or when endovascular therapy is not feasible.

Guideline Must Know: In NOMI, the treatment is physiology-first: correct the precipitating shock/low-flow state, minimize vasoconstrictors when possible, optimize cardiac output, and consider intra-arterial vasodilator infusion (e.g., papaverine) in coordination with IR/vascular when NOMI is suspected/confirmed.

Guideline Must Know: In MVT, many patients can be managed medically with continuous UFH infusion (therapeutic anticoagulation) plus supportive care; escalate to endovascular/surgical options for clinical deterioration, peritonitis, or failure of anticoagulation.

Don’t be falsely reassured by “normal” lactate: lactate may be normal early; trending matters. Worrisome trajectories include rising lactate, increasing anion gap metabolic acidosis, or escalating opioid requirement with persistent severe pain.

Night-float practical differentiation: ischemic colitis often has crampy pain and hematochezia with watershed distribution and is frequently nonoperative unless peritonitis/gangrene; AMI more often presents with sudden severe pain, high-risk vascular history, and rapid deterioration—CTA helps differentiate patterns and directs revascularization.

Hemodynamic strategy nuance: norepinephrine may be needed to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg, but excessive vasoconstriction can worsen splanchnic perfusion (especially NOMI); use the lowest effective dose, consider adding inotropy if low-output, and fix upstream causes (arrhythmia, hypovolemia, sepsis).

Confirm Before Proceed: catheter-directed thrombolysis or high-dose thrombolytics (if considered by IR/vascular) requires careful screening for bleeding risk and recent stroke; do not “green light” without specialist-led risk review and documented contraindication check.

What can wait (after CTA/consults/resuscitation underway): hypercoagulable workup (if unprovoked MVT), long-term antithrombotic plan, atherosclerosis risk optimization, and surveillance imaging after revascularization—these are important but should not delay diagnosis/reperfusion tonight.

Common pitfalls: delaying CTA for “GI workup,” attributing pain to opioid-seeking, giving large doses of opioids that mask peritoneal signs without reassessment, stopping anticoagulation reflexively for minor blood-streaked stool, and failing to call surgery/vascular early when the CT is “pending.”

Communication must-haves on sign-out: suspected etiology (embolus vs thrombosis vs NOMI vs MVT), last normal time/onset, hemodynamic trend (MAP/pressors), acid-base trend (pH, lactate), anticoag status, and consult response times (OR/IR availability).
icu_consult_triggers: Peritonitis on exam or CT signs of transmural infarction (pneumatosis with portal venous gas, free air) or escalating abdominal compartment physiology.
Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg, or rising pressor needs despite ≥30 mL/kg (or individualized) resuscitation.
Rapidly worsening metabolic derangements: lactate ≥4 mmol/L or rising on serial checks, pH <7.30, or new/worsening acute kidney injury with shock.
Escalating respiratory support (new HFNC/NRB, intubation need) or altered mental status in the setting of suspected bowel ischemia/sepsis.
CTA-confirmed arterial occlusion, NOMI with ongoing ischemia, or MVT with clinical deterioration: requires urgent vascular/IR + surgery coordination.

q.st: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) develops sudden, severe diffuse abdominal pain that is “10/10” and out of proportion to a soft abdomen with minimal tenderness. He is afebrile, HR 122/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, RR 22/min. Lactate is 2.1 mmol/L and WBC is 14 x10^9/L. What is the best next step?
o: A. Obtain CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast immediately
B. Order abdominal radiographs and repeat abdominal exam in 4 hours
C. Start a proton pump inhibitor infusion and test for H. pylori
D. Give magnesium citrate and discharge if pain improves
E. Obtain right upper quadrant ultrasound for biliary colic
q.r: Acute mesenteric ischemia must be assumed in severe pain out of proportion to exam, especially with atrial fibrillation, and CTA should be performed without delay to confirm arterial occlusion and guide revascularization. Early lactate can be normal or only mildly elevated, so delaying imaging for serial exams increases risk of bowel infarction. Plain radiographs and ultrasound do not reliably diagnose AMI and should not postpone CTA.

q.st: A 78-year-old woman with diffuse atherosclerosis presents with abrupt severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Exam shows marked pain with minimal tenderness. BP is 92/54 mmHg, HR 118/min. Creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL (baseline unknown). Lactate is 3.8 mmol/L. The team hesitates to order contrast imaging because of kidney injury. What is the best next step?
o: A. Defer contrast studies and obtain noncontrast CT first
B. Obtain CT angiography abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast immediately while resuscitating
C. Start total parenteral nutrition and observe overnight
D. Treat empirically for pancreatitis and reassess after lipase returns
E. Obtain colonoscopy to evaluate for ischemic colitis
q.r: The pitfall is delaying definitive diagnosis for kidney concerns: suspected acute mesenteric ischemia is life-threatening, and CTA should not be delayed when clinical suspicion is high, even with acute kidney injury, because rapid reperfusion decisions depend on vascular imaging. Simultaneous resuscitation (optimize MAP ≥65 mmHg) and early consults are essential; noncontrast CT and colonoscopy can miss or delay actionable arterial findings. What changed the decision here?

m.q: In suspected acute mesenteric ischemia, what is the first-line diagnostic imaging test that should not be delayed?
m.a: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.

m.q: What is the initial anticoagulation typically used when AMI is suspected and there is no major contraindication?
m.a: IV unfractionated heparin, commonly a bolus then continuous infusion titrated to therapeutic aPTT/anti-Xa.

m.q: Name one objective finding that mandates emergent surgical exploration rather than observation.
m.a: Peritonitis on exam or imaging evidence of transmural infarction (e.g., pneumatosis with portal venous gas or free air).

m.q: In NOMI, what is the primary management focus?
m.a: Correct the underlying low-flow/shock state and improve mesenteric perfusion, including minimizing vasoconstrictors when feasible.

Start broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour if septic or high suspicion cholangitis; cover enteric gram-negatives + anaerobes (add enterococcal coverage if healthcare-associated/high risk).
Suspected ascending cholangitis: call GI urgently for biliary decompression; aim ERCP as soon as feasible (do not “wait for MRCP” if unstable).
NPO, antiemetic, analgesia; avoid hypotension from oversedation; correct hypoglycemia and severe electrolyte derangements.
Get RUQ ultrasound first-line; if equivocal and high concern for complications/alternative diagnosis, CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast if renal function permits.
Confirm Before Proceed: anticoagulation reversal, emergent ERCP, or surgery—verify INR/platelets, hemodynamic stability, and consult plan before irreversible steps.
brief_overview: Think in syndromes on nights: (1) acute cholangitis (infection + obstruction), (2) acute cholecystitis (inflamed gallbladder), (3) choledocholithiasis/obstructive jaundice without infection, (4) biliary pancreatitis; the first two can decompensate fast and require early source control.

Guideline Must Know: Acute cholangitis is diagnosed by systemic inflammation + cholestasis + imaging evidence of biliary obstruction/etiology; don’t require Charcot triad—absence of fever/jaundice does not exclude it, especially in elderly, immunosuppressed, or already-antipyretic patients.

Guideline Must Know: For suspected cholangitis, start antibiotics and resuscitation immediately, then prioritize biliary drainage; if moderate–severe disease or not improving rapidly, pursue urgent decompression rather than serial labs and “watchful waiting.”

Guideline Must Know: Severity matters: cholangitis with organ dysfunction (hypotension needing vasopressors, altered mental status, hypoxemia, AKI/oliguria, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia) is severe—treat as sepsis with immediate escalation and plan for urgent drainage.

Guideline Must Know: Acute cholecystitis: RUQ ultrasound is first test; start antibiotics if systemic signs, suspected gangrene/perforation/emphysematous disease, or significant comorbidity; early surgical evaluation is appropriate even if pain improves transiently.

Guideline Must Know: If unstable or high operative risk with acute cholecystitis, gallbladder drainage (percutaneous cholecystostomy) can be a bridge; continue antibiotics and reassess for definitive cholecystectomy once stabilized.

Guideline Must Know: Suspected choledocholithiasis should be risk-stratified to avoid unnecessary ERCP; high-risk features (e.g., stone seen on imaging, ascending cholangitis, or total bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated CBD) generally warrant therapeutic ERCP rather than additional tests.

Guideline Must Know: In intermediate-risk choledocholithiasis (abnormal LFTs, age >55, or CBD dilation without high-risk criteria), use EUS or MRCP for confirmation; avoid diagnostic ERCP due to procedure risk.

Guideline Must Know: Biliary pancreatitis: urgent ERCP is indicated when complicated by cholangitis; otherwise avoid routine urgent ERCP in the first 48 hours unless there is persistent biliary obstruction/choledocholithiasis with worsening cholestasis or clinical deterioration.

What must happen now (night shift): (1) determine instability (hypotension, AMS, lactate, escalating oxygen), (2) obtain RUQ ultrasound and key labs (CBC, CMP, bilirubin fractionation, INR, lipase, lactate), (3) start antibiotics when cholangitis/cholecystitis with systemic illness is suspected, (4) involve GI/surgery early for source control.

What can wait (if stable): repeat imaging (MRCP/EUS), outpatient etiologic workup for mild, resolved biliary colic, and definitive elective cholecystectomy planning after an uncomplicated stone event; document contingency triggers and reassessment timing.

Antibiotic approach (adult inpatient): tailor to severity and acquisition; examples include piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for community-acquired disease; add broader coverage (e.g., cefepime plus metronidazole, or carbapenem) if severe sepsis, prior resistant organisms, or healthcare-associated infection; de-escalate to cultures and clinical response.

Fluids/pressors: treat hypoperfusion like any sepsis—balanced crystalloid, reassess after each bolus (lung exam, urine output, lactate), and use norepinephrine first-line for persistent hypotension; avoid fluid overload in cirrhosis/CHF/ESRD—use smaller boluses and earlier vasopressors with monitoring.

Pitfalls: anchoring on “normal” LFTs early (can lag), missing cholangitis in afebrile/immunosuppressed patients, delaying GI consult until daylight despite rising lactate or confusion, and giving NSAIDs/opioids without monitoring in older adults with borderline respiratory status.

When to call specialists: GI urgently for cholangitis with obstruction or high-risk choledocholithiasis; surgery for acute cholecystitis, gallbladder perforation/gangrene/emphysematous concern, or biliary pancreatitis needing same-admission cholecystectomy after stabilization; ICU for organ dysfunction or escalating support needs.
icu_consult_triggers: MAP <65 mmHg after fluids or need for vasopressors, lactate ≥2 mmol/L with clinical hypoperfusion, or new/worsening altered mental status.
Rising oxygen/ventilatory support (new SpO₂ <90% on ≥6 L/min nasal cannula, need for HFNC/NIV, or impending intubation).
Evidence of severe cholangitis/organ dysfunction: oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h, creatinine rapidly rising, INR ≥1.5 not explained, platelets <100 ×10⁹/L, or bilirubin rapidly climbing with systemic illness.
Imaging/clinical complications: emphysematous cholecystitis, gallbladder perforation, peritonitis, hepatic abscess, or persistent obstruction with sepsis despite antibiotics.
Concern for biliary pancreatitis with severe physiology (SIRS with rising BUN/hematocrit, persistent organ failure) or unclear diagnosis requiring higher-level monitoring.

q.st: A 68-year-old man with known gallstones is admitted for abdominal pain and confusion overnight. He is febrile to 39.2°C, BP 86/52 mmHg after 1 L of crystalloid, HR 118/min, and he is jaundiced. Labs show WBC 18 ×10⁹/L, total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), and lactate 3.8 mmol/L. RUQ ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. He has received broad-spectrum antibiotics.
o: A. Order MRCP in the morning to confirm choledocholithiasis before any procedure
B. Administer additional opioids and observe; antibiotics are sufficient overnight
C. Arrange urgent biliary decompression with ERCP (or percutaneous drainage if ERCP unavailable)
D. Start corticosteroids for presumed autoimmune cholangitis
E. Discontinue antibiotics and wait for blood culture results before further steps
q.r: This presentation is severe acute cholangitis with shock and organ dysfunction, requiring immediate resuscitation plus urgent source control via biliary drainage rather than delayed confirmatory imaging. Early decompression (ERCP preferred when feasible) is key to reversing sepsis; MRCP can be appropriate in stable, intermediate-risk cases but should not delay drainage in unstable patients.

q.st: A 59-year-old woman is admitted for right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. She is afebrile, BP 128/74 mmHg, HR 92/min. Labs show AST 210 U/L, ALT 260 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 190 U/L, and total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones and a common bile duct diameter of 7 mm; no stone is visualized. She has a history of post-ERCP pancreatitis.
o: A. Proceed directly to ERCP tonight for suspected choledocholithiasis
B. Obtain MRCP or EUS to confirm choledocholithiasis before ERCP
C. Give antibiotics and schedule cholecystectomy only; no further biliary evaluation is needed
D. Start heparin infusion for presumed hepatic vein thrombosis
E. Administer tPA for presumed biliary obstruction
q.r: This is intermediate-risk suspected choledocholithiasis (abnormal liver tests and mildly dilated CBD without high-risk criteria), where noninvasive confirmation with MRCP or EUS is preferred to avoid unnecessary ERCP. The pitfall is overusing diagnostic ERCP—especially important here given prior post-ERCP pancreatitis risk.

m.q: In suspected cholangitis with shock, should you wait for MRCP before calling GI for drainage?
m.a: No. Urgent biliary decompression should not be delayed for confirmatory imaging in unstable patients.

m.q: What bilirubin threshold plus CBD dilation places a patient in a high-risk group that generally warrants ERCP without further confirmatory testing?
m.a: Total bilirubin >4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD on imaging.

m.q: In biliary pancreatitis, when is ERCP indicated within 24 hours?
m.a: When acute pancreatitis is complicated by cholangitis.

m.q: First-line imaging test for suspected acute cholecystitis on the ward?
m.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

panic_card: If any red-flag symptoms (hematochezia/melena, iron-deficiency anemia, unintentional weight loss, obstructive symptoms), treat as diagnostic pathway, not “screening”; assess stability and urgency now.
If active bleeding or shock: ABCs, 2 large-bore IVs, type and screen, trend CBC; target MAP ≥65 mmHg and transfuse per clinical context; call GI early if ongoing bleed/instability.
Do not “repeat the stool test” after a positive noninvasive screen; positive FIT/sDNA-FIT requires colonoscopy to complete screening
If inpatient is due/overdue but asymptomatic: prioritize safe discharge follow-up (referral + documented plan); avoid ordering inpatient FIT intended for outpatient screening.
brief_overview: Night-float framing: CRC screening is preventive for asymptomatic, average-risk adults, but you’ll encounter it as “overdue screening,” “positive stool test,” or “chronic iron-deficiency anemia” discovered during admission; your job overnight is to identify red flags, avoid inappropriate inpatient screening, and create a reliable follow-up plan

Guideline Must Know: Average-risk adults should be screened from age 45 through 75; ages 76–85 are selective/individualized based on health, prior screening, and preferences; >85 generally no screening

Guideline Must Know: Acceptable USPSTF strategies include annual FIT, sDNA-FIT every 1–3 years, CT colonography every 5 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years (or every 10 years + annual FIT), or colonoscopy every 10 years; “best test is the one that gets done” after shared decision-making

Guideline Must Know: ACG endorses colonoscopy every 10 years and FIT annually as primary modalities; other options (sDNA-FIT, CT colonography, capsule) are alternatives when colonoscopy/FIT not feasible

Guideline Must Know: Any abnormal non-colonoscopy screening test must be followed by timely diagnostic colonoscopy to complete the screening process; do not substitute repeat FIT or imaging as “confirmation.”

Guideline Must Know: Screening recommendations apply to asymptomatic, average-risk adults (no prior CRC/advanced adenomas, no IBD colitis, no high-risk hereditary syndrome); if symptoms or high-risk history exist, route to diagnostic or high-risk surveillance pathways

What must happen now (night shift): if the admission uncovers concerning features (e.g., new iron-deficiency anemia, overt bleeding, or obstructive symptoms), initiate diagnostic evaluation (CBC trend, iron studies, hemodynamics, consider CT if obstruction suspected) and escalate to GI if unstable or high concern; label it clearly as diagnostic workup, not screening

What can wait until daytime: in stable, asymptomatic patients who are merely overdue, document “CRC screening due” with the preferred modality and place an outpatient referral/order; ensure discharge instructions include the test and the reason (preventive screening) and confirm the patient has a PCP pathway.

Pitfall: Ordering inpatient FIT for “screening” can create false reassurance or confusing positives (hospital diet, acute illness, recent NSAID use, inpatient anticoagulation workups); if a FIT was obtained anyway and is positive, treat it as needing colonoscopy follow-up, not repeat FIT

High-risk family history shortcut for nights: if 1 first-degree relative with CRC or advanced polyp <60, or ≥2 first-degree relatives at any age, screening typically starts at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest diagnosis, with colonoscopy every 5 years; if 1 first-degree relative ≥60, start at age 40 or 10 years before then resume average-risk intervals (often colonoscopy at standard intervals)

Guideline Must Know: Do not overpromise benefit in frail patients: screening benefit is greatest when life expectancy is sufficient (often framed as ~10+ years); for older adults, increased procedure harms (prep dehydration/electrolytes, perforation, sedation events) should be weighed against benefit

Guideline Must Know: A positive stool-based test should be paired with clear documentation of the follow-up plan and timeline (diagnostic colonoscopy); delays reduce the “completed screening” value and can miss lesions

Practical inpatient counseling (1–2 minute script): “You qualify for CRC screening starting at 45. Options include annual FIT or colonoscopy every 10 years. If we use a stool test and it’s positive, the next step is colonoscopy.” Keep it factual, avoid long debates at 2 a.m., and hand off to day team/PCP

Anticoag/antiplatelet pitfall: patients sometimes ask about holding meds for colonoscopy while inpatient; avoid irreversible changes overnight unless a procedure is scheduled—most screening colonoscopies should be outpatient with coordinated periprocedural anticoagulation planning by the proceduralist/ordering clinician.

When the “screening” question is actually cancer concern: unexplained microcytic anemia in an adult male/postmenopausal female or persistent hematochezia should trigger diagnostic evaluation rather than outpatient screening deferral; document clearly to prevent discharge without follow-up
icu_consult_triggers: Hemodynamic instability or ongoing overt GI bleeding: SBP <90, MAP <65 despite fluids, syncope, rising lactate, or escalating transfusion requirement.
Suspected large-bowel obstruction or perforation (severe distention, peritonitis, free air, worsening pain with guarding) requiring urgent imaging and surgical/GI escalation.
Symptomatic anemia with end-organ ischemia or rapid Hb fall (e.g., Hb drop ≥2 g/dL with symptoms) needing urgent evaluation and consult.
New high-risk history suggesting hereditary syndrome (multiple early cancers, very young CRC in family) needing expedited GI/genetics referral planning.

q.st: A 47-year-old man is admitted for cellulitis. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, no family history of colorectal cancer, and no prior colorectal screening. He asks when he should start screening and chooses colonoscopy as his preferred method. What is the recommended screening interval for colonoscopy in an average-risk adult with a normal examination?
o: A. Every 1 year
B. Every 3 years
C. Every 5 years
D. Every 10 years
E. Every 15 years
q.r: For average-risk adults who choose colonoscopy, the recommended screening interval after a normal, high-quality exam is every 10 years per major U.S. guidelines Colonoscopy is one of several acceptable strategies; the key is adherence to an evidence-based interval and completion of follow-up if abnormalities are found.

q.st: A 42-year-old woman is hospitalized for asthma exacerbation. She has no GI symptoms but reports her father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 52. She has never been screened. Which is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening plan?
o: A. Begin screening at age 45 with annual FIT
B. Begin screening now with colonoscopy and repeat every 10 years if normal
C. Begin screening now with colonoscopy and repeat every 5 years if normal
D. Begin screening at age 50 with colonoscopy every 10 years
E. No screening is indicated because she is asymptomatic
q.r: This is a higher-risk family history (first-degree relative with CRC <60), so screening should begin at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest diagnosis (whichever is earlier), using colonoscopy with 5-year intervals if normal The pitfall is treating her as average risk and delaying or using average-risk intervals.

m.q: What is the recommended starting age for average-risk colorectal cancer screening in current USPSTF guidance?
m.a: 45 years for average-risk, asymptomatic adults.

m.q: After a positive FIT done as screening, what is the next required step to complete screening?
m.a: Diagnostic colonoscopy; do not repeat FIT to “confirm.”

m.q: What is the standard interval for screening colonoscopy after a normal exam in an average-risk adult?
m.a: 10 years if the colonoscopy was high quality and normal

m.q: In adults aged 76–85, how should screening decisions be made?
m.a: Selectively/individualized based on overall health, prior screening history, and patient preferences

panic_card: If acute respiratory distress, vomiting, or suspected aspiration: stop feeds now, suction airway, place head of bed 30–45°, give O₂ to goal SpO₂ ≥92% (or 88–92% if chronic hypercapnia), and assess need for ICU/airway protection.

If tube dislodgement or malposition suspected (new cough with feeds, inability to flush, external length change): stop feeds; “Confirm Before Proceed” before use—do not restart feeds or give meds until placement verified per institutional policy (often radiograph for NG/OG).

If hemodynamic instability (rising pressor needs, escalating lactate, mottled/cool extremities): hold enteral feeds until resuscitated; prioritize MAP ≥65 mmHg and perfusion, then reassess for cautious reinitiation.

If refeeding risk with new nutrition (starvation, alcoholism, very low BMI): start low and monitor—give thiamine 100 mg IV/PO now, check/replace K⁺, Mg²⁺, PO₄³⁻ urgently, and avoid rapid calorie escalation.
If hypoglycemia while on tube feeds/insulin: treat immediately with dextrose; if feeds stopped unexpectedly, start dextrose infusion and reduce/hold insulin to prevent recurrent hypoglycemia.
brief_overview: On nights, the highest-yield “enteral feeding” problems are not formula selection but safety: tube position, aspiration risk, feed intolerance, glycemic swings, and electrolyte shifts (especially refeeding), with clear “hold vs continue” logic that avoids reflexive prolonged NPO.

Guideline Must Know: For adults who cannot meet needs orally, enteral nutrition is preferred when the gut works; in critically ill adults, initiate early EN within 24–48 h when appropriate rather than waiting for bowel sounds or flatus, but do not force feeds through shock. (SCCM/ASPEN critical care guidance)

What must happen now: verify access safety (tube location and patency), set aspiration precautions (HOB 30–45°, oral care), define a starting rate, and order monitoring labs for the first 48–72 h if risk of refeeding or intolerance; what can wait: fine-tuning macro goals, specialty formulas, and long-term access decisions (PEG) unless there is an urgent barrier to feeding.

Guideline Must Know: In hemodynamic compromise, hold EN until the patient is fully resuscitated and stable; cautious initiation/reinitiation may be considered during de-escalation of vasopressors, with close monitoring for gut ischemia symptoms. (SCCM/ASPEN critical care guidance)

Practical starting targets (adult inpatient, not a dietitian substitute): start at 10–30 mL/h continuous if uncertain tolerance or high aspiration risk; advance every 8–12 h as tolerated to ordered goal, prioritizing protein delivery over “full calories” in early critical illness when appropriate.

Guideline Must Know: Do not stop feeds for low gastric residual volumes; avoid routine holds for GRV below a high threshold (commonly <500 mL) in the absence of other intolerance signs, because premature interruptions worsen calorie/protein delivery without clear aspiration benefit. (SCCM/ASPEN critical care guidance)

Feeding intolerance is a syndrome, not a number: concerning findings include recurrent emesis, increasing abdominal distention/pain, absent bowel gas with worsening exam, high NG output, rising lactate, or new vasopressor escalation; respond by reducing rate, switching to continuous, adding a prokinetic, and considering postpyloric access rather than repeated full stoppages.

Guideline Must Know: If aspiration risk is high (ongoing vomiting, poor airway protection, recurrent aspiration, intolerance of gastric feeds), consider postpyloric feeding and use a continuous infusion strategy; always keep HOB elevated unless contraindicated. (SCCM/ASPEN and ASPEN safe practices)

Refeeding syndrome is the classic night-float pitfall: risk is highest with little/no intake for several days, alcoholism, significant weight loss, very low BMI, and baseline electrolyte depletion; watch for hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia after nutrition starts, plus edema, arrhythmia, weakness, and respiratory failure.

Guideline Must Know: In high-risk refeeding, give thiamine 100 mg before and during early feeding, start at low calories (often ~10 kcal/kg/day in very high-risk states), and monitor/replace PO₄³⁻, K⁺, Mg²⁺ frequently (e.g., at least daily, often q12–24 h initially) while slowly advancing. (NICE CG32; ASPEN refeeding consensus/safe practices)

Glycemic management: tube feeds behave like continuous carbohydrate infusion; prevent hypoglycemia by matching insulin to feed delivery and creating a “what if feeds stop” plan (dextrose rescue). Target inpatient glucose commonly 140–180 mg/dL for most nonpregnant adults, avoiding tight control that increases hypoglycemia. (ADA inpatient standards)

Guideline Must Know: Use standardized protocols/order sets for inpatient dysglycemia; check A1C if not available within 3 months in patients with diabetes or significant hyperglycemia, and prefer scheduled basal plus nutritional/correction insulin over sliding scale alone. (ADA inpatient standards)

Meds through tubes are a frequent source of clogging and underdosing: flush before/after each medication and avoid crushing extended-release/enteric-coated products; if the tube clogs, use warm water flushes first and reassess medication formulation rather than repeated forceful flushing that risks tube disruption. (ASPEN safe practices)

Common “can’t eat” orders at night: avoid prolonged NPO for routine imaging/procedures without clear instructions; if a procedure is uncertain, consider a time-limited hold with a restart plan (and dextrose/insulin adjustments) rather than an open-ended stop.

When to call for help: early dietitian/nutrition support consult for severe malnutrition, complex electrolyte instability, or prolonged intolerance; GI/IR for difficult access or recurrent dislodgement; ICU if feeding intolerance occurs with shock physiology, rising lactate, or suspected bowel ischemia.

Red flags suggesting bowel ischemia or catastrophic intolerance (ICU/STAT evaluation): abdominal pain out of proportion, rigid abdomen, persistent lactic acidosis, escalating pressors, GI bleeding, or pneumatosis/portal venous gas on imaging; stop EN and treat as a medical emergency.
icu_consult_triggers: New or worsening respiratory failure during feeds (increasing O₂ needs, recurrent emesis/aspiration, need for NIV/HFNC or impending intubation).
Hemodynamic instability with EN (escalating vasopressors, MAP <65 mmHg despite resuscitation, rising lactate, or signs of poor perfusion).
Suspected bowel ischemia or perforation (severe/worsening abdominal pain, peritonitis, GI bleeding, lactate rising, imaging concern such as pneumatosis).

Severe refeeding physiology after starting nutrition (symptomatic arrhythmia, weakness/respiratory failure, or refractory PO₄³⁻ <0.5 mmol/L or equivalent severe hypophosphatemia with clinical instability).
Recurrent tube malposition/dislodgement or inability to safely administer meds/feeds despite bedside troubleshooting (GI/IR consult for definitive access).
