q.st: A 62-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted for severe pancreatitis. He has had minimal oral intake for 8 days. On night float, a nasogastric tube is placed and continuous enteral feeding is ordered to start immediately at the goal rate. His baseline labs show potassium 3.3 mmol/L, magnesium 0.55 mmol/L, and phosphate 0.7 mmol/L. He is hemodynamically stable on room air. Which of the following is the best next step to reduce the most serious complication of initiating nutrition?
o: A. Start feeds at the goal rate and recheck electrolytes in 48 hours
B. Administer thiamine now, replete electrolytes, and start feeds at a low rate with close monitoring
C. Hold all nutrition for 72 hours and give only IV fluids
D. Switch to bolus gastric feeds to reduce aspiration risk
E. Start insulin infusion to maintain glucose 80–110 mg/dL during feeding initiation
q.r: This patient is high risk for refeeding syndrome given prolonged poor intake and baseline electrolyte depletion; thiamine plus aggressive replacement and slow caloric advancement reduces life-threatening hypophosphatemia-related arrhythmia and respiratory failure. Guideline-based nutrition support emphasizes cautious initiation with frequent monitoring in high-risk patients rather than immediate goal feeding. Tight glucose control increases hypoglycemia risk and is not recommended for most inpatients.

q.st: A 70-year-old woman with septic shock is in the ICU on norepinephrine at 0.25 µg/kg/min with rising lactate and cool extremities. A new order is placed to start continuous enteral feeds overnight because she has been NPO for 2 days. Her abdomen is soft but mildly distended. Which is the best next step regarding enteral feeding?
o: A. Start full-rate gastric feeds now to prevent gut mucosal atrophy
B. Start trophic feeds now and advance rapidly every 2 hours regardless of pressor dose
C. Hold enteral feeds until she is adequately resuscitated and vasopressor requirements are stable or decreasing
D. Switch immediately to bolus feeds to improve tolerance
E. Place a postpyloric tube and start full-rate feeds immediately despite shock
q.r: Enteral feeding should be withheld in hemodynamic instability until resuscitation and perfusion are adequate; escalating vasopressors and rising lactate raise concern for impaired gut perfusion and ischemia risk. The pitfall is assuming “some feeds are always safe” during active shock; even trophic feeding requires caution and close monitoring once pressors are stable or de-escalating. What changed the decision here?

m.q: Should you restart a newly placed NG/OG tube for feeds before confirmation of placement?
m.a: No. Do not use the tube for feeds or medications until placement is verified per policy (often radiographic confirmation for NG/OG).

m.q: What head-of-bed angle reduces aspiration risk during tube feeding?
m.a: Maintain 30–45° elevation unless contraindicated.

m.q: In a high-risk refeeding patient, which electrolytes must be monitored closely after starting nutrition?
m.a: Phosphate, potassium, and magnesium should be checked and replaced frequently during initiation and advancement.

m.q: What is a typical inpatient glucose target range for most nonpregnant adults receiving enteral feeds?
m.a: 140–180 mg/dL is a common target range to reduce complications while minimizing hypoglycemia.

PRE.st: A 61-year-old man with no known liver disease presents with melena and lightheadedness. BP is 102/64 mmHg, HR 108/min. Hemoglobin is 6.4 g/dL, INR 1.0. Two large-bore IVs are placed and crystalloid is running. Which of the following is the most appropriate transfusion threshold for this hemodynamically improving patient?
o: A. Transfuse to maintain hemoglobin ≥10 g/dL
B. Transfuse when hemoglobin is <7 g/dL
C. Transfuse only if systolic blood pressure remains below 90 mmHg
D. Withhold transfusion until endoscopy confirms the bleeding source
E. Transfuse 4 units of fresh frozen plasma before any red blood cells
PRE.r: Guidelines support a restrictive transfusion strategy for hemodynamically stable UGIB, recommending RBC transfusion when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL. Transfusing to ≥10 g/dL is a liberal strategy associated with worse outcomes. FFP is not indicated with a normal INR, and transfusion should not be withheld pending endoscopy when the patient meets threshold.

PRE.st: A 70-year-old woman presents with large-volume hematochezia. She is tachycardic (HR 118/min) and hypotensive (BP 84/50 mmHg) despite 2 liters of crystalloid. She continues to pass bright red blood. Which imaging modality is most appropriate to rapidly localize the bleeding source?
o: A. Urgent colonoscopy after rapid bowel preparation
B. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
C. Tagged red blood cell scintigraphy
D. Abdominal plain radiograph
E. Capsule endoscopy
PRE.r: In hemodynamically significant ongoing lower GI bleeding, CT angiography is the preferred rapid localization test and can directly guide interventional radiology embolization. Colonoscopy requires bowel prep and is limited in active brisk bleeding. Tagged RBC scan is less readily available and slower. Plain films and capsule endoscopy are not appropriate for acute localization.

PRE.st: A 48-year-old woman is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Lipase is 5× the upper limit of normal. She is hemodynamically stable after IV fluids and her pain is improving. Which of the following is the recommended approach to nutrition in the first 24 hours?
o: A. Keep strictly NPO for at least 72 hours to rest the pancreas
B. Start early oral feeding as tolerated within 24 hours
C. Begin total parenteral nutrition immediately
D. Start a clear liquid diet only after lipase normalizes
E. Defer all nutrition until contrast CT confirms no necrosis
PRE.r: Guidelines recommend early oral feeding as tolerated within 24 hours for mild acute pancreatitis, which improves outcomes compared with prolonged NPO. Routine early CT is not indicated, and parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate enteral feeding. Waiting for lipase normalization is not recommended.

PRE.st: A 50-year-old man with heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice, AST 320 U/L, ALT 140 U/L (AST:ALT >2:1), total bilirubin 12 mg/dL, and INR 1.8. He has mild confusion but no asterixis. His acetaminophen level is undetectable. What is the most important initial step in management?
o: A. Start prednisone immediately without further evaluation
B. Start N-acetylcysteine and evaluate for acute liver failure criteria including encephalopathy assessment
C. Discharge with outpatient hepatology follow-up since acetaminophen is negative
D. Transfuse fresh frozen plasma to normalize the INR
E. Start empiric antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
PRE.r: With INR ≥1.5 and possible encephalopathy, acute liver failure must be evaluated urgently. N-acetylcysteine has benefit in non-acetaminophen acute liver failure and should be started while the workup proceeds. Routine FFP to correct INR is not recommended without active bleeding. Starting steroids without full assessment or dismissing the presentation would be premature.

PRE.st: A 35-year-old woman with no known liver disease presents with confusion and vomiting. AST is 7,500 U/L, ALT 8,200 U/L, INR 2.6, and glucose 52 mg/dL. She may have taken over-the-counter cold medicines containing acetaminophen. Which combination of actions is most appropriate immediately?
o: A. Start IV N-acetylcysteine, treat hypoglycemia with dextrose, and arrange ICU/transplant center consultation
B. Observe on the general floor with q12h labs until acetaminophen level returns
C. Give fresh frozen plasma to correct INR and start lactulose only
D. Start corticosteroids for presumed autoimmune hepatitis
E. Administer activated charcoal and plan outpatient follow-up
PRE.r: This patient meets criteria for acute liver failure (INR >1.5, encephalopathy, no prior cirrhosis) with possible acetaminophen exposure. IV NAC should be started immediately without waiting for levels, hypoglycemia must be corrected with continuous dextrose, and early transplant-center involvement is critical. Routine FFP without bleeding is not indicated, and floor observation is unsafe.

PRE.st: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. BP is 90/54 mmHg and HR is 116/min. You suspect variceal bleeding. After starting crystalloid resuscitation, which two medications should be initiated immediately before endoscopy?
o: A. Pantoprazole infusion and metoclopramide
B. Octreotide infusion and ceftriaxone
C. Lactulose and rifaximin
D. Propranolol and spironolactone
E. Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma
PRE.r: The initial management bundle for suspected acute variceal hemorrhage includes a vasoactive agent (octreotide) plus antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone), started immediately before endoscopy. These medications reduce rebleeding and infection-related mortality. PPIs are for nonvariceal bleeding, and propranolol/spironolactone are for chronic management, not acute hemorrhage.

PRE.st: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis is admitted for confusion and asterixis. Her ammonia level is elevated. She has not had a bowel movement in 4 days and recently started oxycodone. Which is the recommended first-line treatment?
o: A. Rifaximin monotherapy
B. Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools per day
C. Protein restriction to 0.6 g/kg/day
D. Flumazenil infusion
E. IV lorazepam for agitation
PRE.r: Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools per day is the recommended first-line treatment for episodic overt hepatic encephalopathy. Rifaximin is add-on therapy for recurrence prevention, not initial monotherapy. Protein restriction is harmful, flumazenil is not standard therapy, and benzodiazepines worsen encephalopathy.

PRE.st: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with fever and abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis shows 800 WBC/µL with 85% neutrophils. Cultures are pending. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: A. Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics
B. Start ceftriaxone IV and administer IV albumin
C. Start oral ciprofloxacin and discharge home
D. Repeat paracentesis in 24 hours to confirm the cell count
E. Start IV metronidazole alone
PRE.r: An ascitic PMN count ≥250 cells/µL establishes the diagnosis of SBP and mandates immediate empiric antibiotics (typically a third-generation cephalosporin like ceftriaxone) plus IV albumin for renal protection. Culture confirmation is not required before treatment. Oral antibiotics and discharge are inappropriate for acute SBP with systemic symptoms.

PRE.st: A 28-year-old man with ulcerative colitis presents with 12 bloody stools per day, HR 106/min, T 38.1°C, and hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL. Stool C. difficile testing is negative. Which is the most appropriate initial inpatient therapy?
o: A. Oral mesalamine 4.8 g daily
B. Methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily
C. Infliximab 5 mg/kg IV immediately
D. Loperamide for symptom control
E. Oral budesonide 9 mg daily
PRE.r: This presentation meets criteria for acute severe ulcerative colitis (≥6 bloody stools/day plus systemic toxicity). IV corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily) are the standard initial therapy. Infliximab is rescue therapy for steroid non-responders. Loperamide is contraindicated in severe colitis due to ileus/megacolon risk. Oral mesalamine and budesonide are insufficient for severe disease.

PRE.st: A 74-year-old man develops 8 watery stools over 24 hours on hospital day 5 after completing antibiotics for pneumonia. WBC is 12,800/µL and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. C. difficile testing is positive. Which is the preferred initial treatment?
o: A. Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours
B. Fidaxomicin 200 mg orally twice daily for 10 days
C. Vancomycin 500 mg orally every 6 hours plus IV metronidazole
D. Loperamide and probiotics only
E. Fecal microbiota transplantation
PRE.r: For an initial nonsevere CDI episode, fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days is the guideline-preferred therapy, with oral vancomycin 125 mg QID as an acceptable alternative. The fulminant regimen (vancomycin 500 mg Q6H + IV metronidazole) is reserved for patients with shock, ileus, or megacolon. Antimotility agents are contraindicated, and FMT is for recurrent CDI prevention.

PRE.st: A 65-year-old man on daily naproxen presents with melena. After resuscitation and hemodynamic stabilization, upper endoscopy reveals a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel that is successfully treated. Which post-endoscopic acid suppression regimen is recommended?
o: A. Oral omeprazole 20 mg once daily
B. High-dose IV PPI for 72 hours, then twice-daily oral PPI for 2 weeks
C. Oral H2-receptor antagonist for 4 weeks
D. Sucralfate four times daily with no acid suppression
E. No acid suppression needed after successful endoscopic therapy
PRE.r: After endoscopic hemostasis of a high-risk bleeding ulcer (visible vessel), guidelines recommend high-dose IV PPI therapy for 72 hours followed by twice-daily oral PPI for 2 weeks to reduce rebleeding risk. Standard-dose once-daily PPI or H2-blockers alone are insufficient for this high-risk scenario.

PRE.st: A 55-year-old man reports 3 months of heartburn and sour taste without dysphagia, weight loss, or GI bleeding. His cardiac workup is negative. Which is the best initial management?
o: A. Urgent upper endoscopy tonight
B. Empiric PPI once daily 30–60 minutes before a meal for 8 weeks
C. Barium swallow as the first diagnostic test
D. Start baclofen nightly
E. 24-hour pH monitoring before any treatment
PRE.r: For classic GERD symptoms without alarm features, guidelines recommend an empiric 8-week trial of a once-daily PPI taken 30–60 minutes before a meal as the initial step. Endoscopy is reserved for alarm symptoms (dysphagia, bleeding, weight loss). Barium swallow, pH monitoring, and baclofen are not first-line approaches.

PRE.st: A 36-year-old woman with 8 months of diarrhea, bloating, and iron-deficiency anemia is being evaluated. She eats a normal diet including wheat. Which initial diagnostic test strategy is most appropriate?
o: A. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping
B. Tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA
C. Stool calprotectin only
D. Start a gluten-free diet and reassess symptoms in 4 weeks
E. Anti-saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)
PRE.r: First-line celiac screening in adults on a gluten-containing diet is tTG-IgA plus total IgA to identify IgA deficiency that would invalidate IgA-based testing. HLA genotyping is mainly useful to rule out celiac when patients are already gluten-free. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing reduces diagnostic sensitivity.

PRE.st: A 32-year-old woman develops sudden bloody diarrhea with severe cramps after eating a hamburger. She is febrile to 38.3°C and hemodynamically stable. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: A. Start empiric azithromycin and loperamide
B. Send stool testing for Shiga toxin-producing organisms and provide supportive care without antibiotics
C. Start high-dose oral vancomycin for presumed C. difficile
D. Administer prednisone for presumed IBD flare
E. Give bismuth subsalicylate and discharge
PRE.r: Bloody diarrhea with severe cramps after ground beef exposure raises concern for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). Guidelines recommend testing for Shiga toxin and avoiding empiric antibiotics in suspected STEC due to potential increased risk of HUS. Antimotility agents are contraindicated in inflammatory/bloody diarrhea.

PRE.st: A 44-year-old immunocompetent man has 6 weeks of watery, nonbloody diarrhea without weight loss or fever. Labs are normal. Which single stool pathogen test is specifically recommended by AGA guidelines?
o: A. Stool culture for Salmonella and Shigella
B. Stool test for Giardia
C. Stool ova and parasites (3 specimens)
D. C. difficile PCR
E. Cryptosporidium antigen
PRE.r: AGA guidelines specifically recommend testing for Giardia in adults with chronic watery diarrhea because it is common and readily treatable. Routine broad ova and parasite testing without high-risk travel exposure is not recommended as a first-line strategy. C. difficile testing is appropriate for acute presentations with antibiotic exposure.

PRE.st: A 60-year-old man is admitted for lymphoma and is scheduled to start rituximab. Pre-treatment labs show: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, total anti-HBc positive. ALT is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: A. No action needed; anti-HBc positivity alone is not clinically significant
B. Begin entecavir prophylaxis before rituximab
C. Administer hepatitis B vaccine and proceed with chemotherapy
D. Start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir
E. Check HCV RNA only
PRE.r: Anti-HBc positivity indicates prior HBV exposure and carries significant risk of HBV reactivation with anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab). Guidelines recommend prophylactic antiviral therapy with a high-barrier agent (entecavir or tenofovir) before initiating immunosuppression. Vaccination does not prevent reactivation from occult HBV, and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir treats HCV, not HBV.

PRE.st: A 73-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) develops sudden severe abdominal pain that is out of proportion to his soft, minimally tender abdomen. Lactate is 2.0 mmol/L and WBC is 13,000/µL. What is the best next diagnostic step?
o: A. Abdominal plain radiographs and serial exams every 4 hours
B. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
C. Right upper quadrant ultrasound
D. Colonoscopy to evaluate for ischemic colitis
E. Upper endoscopy
PRE.r: Acute mesenteric ischemia should be assumed with severe pain out of proportion to exam in a patient with atrial fibrillation. CTA is the first-line diagnostic test and should not be delayed. Early lactate can be normal or mildly elevated and does not exclude the diagnosis. Plain radiographs and serial exams increase risk of bowel infarction by delaying diagnosis.

PRE.st: A 66-year-old man with known gallstones presents with fever (39.1°C), jaundice, confusion, and BP 88/54 mmHg. WBC is 19,000/µL, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and lactate 3.5 mmol/L. RUQ ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. Broad-spectrum antibiotics have been started. What is the most important next intervention?
o: A. Schedule MRCP in the morning to confirm the diagnosis
B. Arrange urgent biliary decompression via ERCP
C. Start corticosteroids for autoimmune cholangitis
D. Continue antibiotics alone and observe
E. Perform cholecystectomy tonight
PRE.r: This is severe acute cholangitis with shock and organ dysfunction, requiring urgent source control via biliary drainage (ERCP preferred). Delayed confirmatory imaging like MRCP should not postpone drainage in an unstable patient. Antibiotics alone are insufficient without source control in severe cholangitis.

PRE.st: A 48-year-old asymptomatic man with no family history of colorectal cancer asks about screening. He has never been screened. What is the recommended starting age and interval if he chooses colonoscopy?
o: A. Start at age 50, repeat every 5 years
B. Start at age 45, repeat every 10 years if normal
C. Start at age 40, repeat every 3 years
D. Start at age 50, repeat every 10 years
E. Start at age 55, repeat every 15 years
PRE.r: Current USPSTF and ACG guidelines recommend beginning average-risk colorectal cancer screening at age 45. For colonoscopy, the recommended interval after a normal, high-quality exam is every 10 years. The previous starting age of 50 was updated in 2021.

PRE.st: A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has had minimal oral intake for 10 days. Enteral feeding is initiated via nasogastric tube. Baseline labs show K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ 0.5 mmol/L, and phosphate 0.6 mmol/L. What is the most important step to reduce the risk of the most serious complication?
o: A. Start feeds at goal rate immediately and recheck labs in 48 hours
B. Give thiamine, aggressively replete electrolytes, and start feeds at a low rate with close monitoring
C. Hold all nutrition for 5 days until electrolytes normalize
D. Start total parenteral nutrition instead of enteral feeds
E. Start insulin infusion targeting glucose 80–110 mg/dL
PRE.r: This patient is at high risk for refeeding syndrome. Guidelines recommend giving thiamine before and during early feeding, aggressively repleting phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, and starting feeds at a low rate with frequent electrolyte monitoring. Immediate goal-rate feeding risks life-threatening hypophosphatemia. Tight glucose control increases hypoglycemia risk.

POST.st: A 57-year-old man with known cirrhosis and prior variceal banding presents with large-volume hematemesis. BP is 86/50 mmHg, HR 126/min. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, INR 1.9, platelets 72,000/mm³. He is intermittently confused. Octreotide and ceftriaxone are started and 1 unit of PRBCs is transfusing. The team considers giving FFP to 'correct the INR' before endoscopy. What is the best approach to his coagulopathy?
o: A. Give 4 units of FFP to normalize INR before endoscopy
B. Avoid routine FFP; focus on hemodynamics and source control via urgent endoscopy
C. Give vitamin K 10 mg IV and delay endoscopy 24 hours for effect
D. Transfuse platelets to >150,000/mm³ before any intervention
E. Start therapeutic heparin to prevent portal vein thrombosis
POST.r: In variceal bleeding with cirrhosis, routine INR correction with plasma is not a resuscitation endpoint and can worsen portal pressures and volume overload. Guidelines emphasize hemodynamic stabilization and source control via urgent endoscopy rather than targeting a specific INR. Platelet transfusion to >150,000 is excessive, and heparin is contraindicated during active hemorrhage.

POST.st: A 62-year-old woman on aspirin 81 mg for secondary cardiovascular prevention (prior MI) presents with hematochezia that self-resolves. She is hemodynamically stable. Colonoscopy reveals a diverticular bleeding site that is successfully treated with endoscopic clips. When should aspirin be resumed?
o: A. Never; aspirin should be permanently discontinued after GI bleeding
B. After 30 days to allow complete mucosal healing
C. On the day endoscopic hemostasis is confirmed
D. Only after a repeat colonoscopy in 3 months confirms healing
E. Switch permanently to clopidogrel to avoid further bleeding
POST.r: For patients on aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention, guidelines recommend resuming aspirin promptly once endoscopic hemostasis is confirmed, as cardiovascular risk from interruption outweighs rebleeding risk. Permanently stopping aspirin in secondary prevention carries significant thrombotic risk. Switching to clopidogrel does not reduce GI bleeding risk.

POST.st: A 70-year-old woman with HFrEF (EF 20%) is admitted with acute pancreatitis. BP is 88/52 mmHg, HR 120/min, SpO₂ 89% on 4 L NC with bibasilar crackles. She received 2 L of lactated Ringer's in the ED. BUN is rising and urine output is low. What is the best next step?
o: A. Continue aggressive fluid boluses until urine output normalizes
B. Start prophylactic antibiotics for suspected severe pancreatitis
C. Transfer to ICU for goal-directed resuscitation with careful titration and vasopressors if MAP remains <65 mmHg
D. Order immediate CT to stage necrosis
E. Start TPN immediately
POST.r: The nuance is avoiding over-resuscitation in a patient with severe cardiac dysfunction. Guidelines support goal-directed fluids with frequent reassessment, but with significant heart failure, continued large boluses risk worsening pulmonary edema. Persistent MAP <65 mmHg after appropriate fluid trial warrants ICU-level monitoring and vasopressors. Prophylactic antibiotics and routine early CT are not recommended.

POST.st: A 64-year-old woman on chronic warfarin for atrial fibrillation is admitted with abdominal discomfort and dark urine. AST is 980 U/L, ALT 1100 U/L, total bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL, and INR 3.1. She is fully oriented with normal mental status and no asterixis. She took her usual warfarin today. How should you evaluate whether she has acute liver failure?
o: A. Diagnose acute liver failure and arrange emergent transfer based on INR alone
B. Attribute the INR entirely to warfarin and ignore hepatic synthetic function
C. Assess encephalopathy carefully and interpret INR in context; trend INR off warfarin and check factor V or fibrinogen
D. Give FFP to normalize INR and repeat labs in the morning
E. Start lactulose immediately because any INR elevation implies encephalopathy
POST.r: The key analytical step is recognizing that warfarin independently elevates INR, making it unreliable as a sole marker of hepatic synthetic failure. Acute liver failure requires both INR ≥1.5 AND encephalopathy. The correct approach is careful mental status assessment plus trending INR after holding warfarin and using additional synthesis markers (factor V, fibrinogen) to differentiate drug effect from liver failure.

POST.st: A 52-year-old man with acute liver failure is intubated in the ICU. INR is 3.1, platelets 28,000/µL, fibrinogen 1.6 g/L. He has no active bleeding. The team asks about pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis since 'his INR is already high.' What is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis?
o: A. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
B. Unfractionated heparin 5,000 units SC q8h
C. No prophylaxis needed because elevated INR means auto-anticoagulation
D. Mechanical prophylaxis with sequential compression devices only
E. Give FFP first, then start enoxaparin
POST.r: A common pitfall is assuming elevated INR means the patient is 'auto-anticoagulated' — ALF patients can still develop thrombosis. However, with platelets at 28,000/µL, pharmacologic prophylaxis carries significant bleeding risk. Mechanical prophylaxis with SCDs is the safest option while reassessing platelet counts. Correcting INR with FFP solely to enable heparin is not recommended.

POST.st: A 62-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis is found overnight to be progressively somnolent and confused with asterixis. She is intermittently vomiting. Vitals are stable and SpO₂ is 94% on room air. The nurse requests lactulose. What is the best immediate next step?
o: A. Give lactulose orally immediately
B. Place an NG tube and give lactulose without further evaluation
C. Secure the airway first, then administer enteral lactulose targeting 2–3 soft stools/day
D. Give IV benzodiazepines for agitation
E. Order screening endoscopy before treating
POST.r: The analytical challenge is recognizing aspiration risk. With depressed mental status (somnolence) and active vomiting, giving enteral lactulose without first addressing airway protection risks aspiration. The correct sequence is airway protection first, then lactulose. Benzodiazepines worsen encephalopathy, and endoscopy is not indicated before treating HE.

POST.st: A 68-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis presents with acute confusion. She is somnolent but arousable, has no asterixis, and her family says 'this looks like her prior hepatic encephalopathy.' Vitals are stable. Her plasma ammonia returns normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: A. Treat with lactulose only and defer all other workup
B. Stop further evaluation because normal ammonia excludes all causes of delirium
C. Re-evaluate for alternative causes of encephalopathy including glucose, electrolytes, infection assessment, and neuroimaging if indicated
D. Start high-dose protein restriction
E. Start prophylactic rifaximin solely because she has a history of TIPS
POST.r: A normal ammonia level should prompt diagnostic re-evaluation rather than anchoring on the HE diagnosis. Guidelines emphasize that HE is a diagnosis of exclusion, and normal ammonia calls it into question. The correct analytical approach is systematic evaluation for alternative causes (metabolic, infectious, structural) while maintaining clinical vigilance. Protein restriction is harmful, and prophylaxis for TIPS alone is not recommended.

POST.st: A 65-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis and recurrent SBP is admitted from a skilled nursing facility with fever and abdominal pain. She takes daily norfloxacin prophylaxis. BP is 96/58 mmHg after 1 L crystalloid, HR 112/min. Paracentesis shows PMN 600 cells/µL. Which empiric antibiotic is most appropriate?
o: A. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
B. Ampicillin-sulbactam IV
C. Piperacillin-tazobactam IV with prompt de-escalation when cultures return
D. Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole only
E. No antibiotics until culture results
POST.r: This healthcare-associated SBP with quinolone prophylaxis exposure increases the likelihood of resistant organisms. Standard community-acquired coverage (ceftriaxone) may be inadequate. Broader empiric therapy with planned de-escalation is appropriate when severity features and MDRO risk factors are present. Oral antibiotics are insufficient in this unstable presentation.

POST.st: A 60-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis on azathioprine presents with 6 days of worsening watery diarrhea and new hematochezia. HR 112/min, T 38.0°C. CT shows diffuse colitis without perforation. Stool testing returns positive for C. difficile. What is the best next step?
o: A. Start methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily for presumed ASUC
B. Start oral vancomycin 125 mg q6h and hold escalation of immunosuppression until infection is addressed
C. Start infliximab 5 mg/kg IV tonight
D. Start loperamide and oral rehydration only
E. Perform colonoscopy with full bowel prep tonight
POST.r: The analytical challenge is recognizing an infectious colitis mimicking an IBD flare. A positive C. difficile test shifts first-line management to targeted antibiotic therapy before escalating immunosuppression. Treating with steroids or biologics in the setting of active CDI worsens outcomes. This demonstrates why infection must always be excluded in suspected IBD flares.

POST.st: A 66-year-old woman with CKD (baseline creatinine 2.0 mg/dL) is admitted with abdominal pain and confusion. She has minimal stool output, nausea, distension, and diffuse tenderness. BP 86/54 mmHg after 2 L crystalloid, HR 118/min. WBC 28,000/µL, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. CT shows diffuse colitis with colonic dilation and ileus. Stool testing is pending. Which antimicrobial regimen is best?
o: A. Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID only
B. Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID only
C. Vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG Q6H plus metronidazole 500 mg IV Q8H, and add vancomycin 500 mg PR Q6H
D. Metronidazole 500 mg PO TID only
E. Defer CDI therapy until test results return
POST.r: This is fulminant CDI (shock with ileus/megacolon features). The analytical key is recognizing that ileus necessitates rectal vancomycin to improve colonic drug delivery, in addition to high-dose enteral vancomycin and systemic metronidazole. Lower-dose or single-agent regimens are inadequate for fulminant disease, and waiting for test results risks further deterioration.

POST.st: A 72-year-old woman with prior MI takes aspirin 81 mg daily for secondary prevention. She is admitted for hematemesis. After resuscitation and successful endoscopic hemostasis of a bleeding duodenal ulcer, the team debates the antiplatelet plan. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: A. Stop aspirin permanently because it caused the ulcer
B. Hold aspirin for 30 days to allow mucosal healing
C. Resume aspirin as soon as possible after confirmed hemostasis with concurrent PPI therapy
D. Switch to clopidogrel permanently and stop PPI
E. Start therapeutic heparin bridging while aspirin is held
POST.r: In secondary cardiovascular prevention, guidelines support early resumption of aspirin after endoscopic hemostasis because cardiovascular risk from interruption is high. Co-therapy with PPI reduces recurrent ulcer bleeding. Permanent discontinuation or prolonged holds carry unacceptable thrombotic risk. Clopidogrel is not safer for GI bleeding, and heparin bridging is not indicated for antiplatelet interruption.

POST.st: A 68-year-old woman on alendronate is admitted for cellulitis. At 2 AM she develops sudden severe odynophagia and substernal pain after taking bedtime pills with a small sip of water while lying flat. She is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and has no drooling. What is the best next step?
o: A. Give a large oral water challenge to push the pills through
B. Keep NPO, start PPI, provide analgesia, and stop the offending medication
C. Start IV thrombolysis for esophageal ischemia
D. Place a nasogastric tube for decompression
E. Start high-dose oral steroids
POST.r: This is classic pill esophagitis from alendronate taken recumbent with inadequate water. The correct management is stopping the offending agent, providing acid suppression (PPI), analgesia, and avoiding further esophageal trauma. Forced oral intake or NG tube placement risks worsening mucosal injury. This requires recognizing the mechanism of injury to guide safe management.

POST.st: A 50-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and iron-deficiency anemia started a gluten-free diet 3 months ago on her own and reports partial improvement. She is admitted for syncope with orthostatic hypotension. You need to clarify whether she has celiac disease. Which test is most useful in this clinical context?
o: A. Tissue transglutaminase IgA only
B. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping
C. Start oral budesonide for presumed refractory celiac disease
D. Diagnose celiac based on symptom improvement alone
E. Perform duodenal biopsies immediately without considering diet status
POST.r: When a patient has already been on a gluten-free diet, serology and biopsy may have normalized, reducing their diagnostic value. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping is most useful here because a negative result effectively rules out celiac disease regardless of diet status, while a positive result is non-diagnostic and may prompt a supervised gluten challenge. The analytical pitfall is assuming symptom improvement alone confirms the diagnosis.

POST.st: A 70-year-old man hospitalized for pneumonia has received ceftriaxone for 5 days. Overnight he develops 6 watery stools, T 38.6°C, WBC 18,500/µL, and creatinine rises from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL. No peritoneal signs are present. What is the best next step?
o: A. Give loperamide and observe
B. Start oral vancomycin and place contact enteric precautions while sending C. difficile testing
C. Start ciprofloxacin for empiric bacterial gastroenteritis
D. Order urgent colonoscopy to confirm pseudomembranes
E. Send stool ova and parasite exam and defer therapy
POST.r: This clinical scenario (post-antibiotic diarrhea with fever, leukocytosis, and AKI) has high probability of CDI. The analytical step is recognizing severity markers (rising creatinine, high WBC) that warrant prompt empiric treatment and isolation rather than waiting for results. Antimotility agents are contraindicated with suspected CDI, and colonoscopy is not needed to initiate therapy.

POST.st: A 74-year-old woman taking a PPI and ibuprofen daily has 3 months of watery diarrhea including nocturnal episodes. Colonoscopy showed normal-appearing mucosa. Labs including hemoglobin and albumin are normal. What is the best next step to establish a diagnosis?
o: A. Reassure her that a normal colonoscopy rules out colitis
B. Start empiric loperamide as definitive therapy
C. Obtain random colonic biopsies to evaluate for microscopic colitis
D. Order ESR and CRP to screen for IBD
E. Start empiric vancomycin for C. difficile
POST.r: The analytical challenge is recognizing that microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea (often nocturnal) with a grossly normal colon — diagnosis requires colonic biopsies. PPI and NSAID use are known triggers. The pitfall is assuming a normal-appearing colonoscopy excludes colitis. ESR/CRP are not recommended as IBD screening tools in chronic watery diarrhea pathways.

POST.st: A 56-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is admitted for hypoxemic respiratory failure. The team plans to start prednisone 60 mg daily tonight with a slow taper over months. HBV labs return: HBsAg positive, anti-HBs negative, total anti-HBc positive. ALT is 78 U/L. HBV DNA is pending. What is the best next step?
o: A. Start tenofovir or entecavir now while steroids begin
B. Delay steroids until HBV DNA results return
C. Give hepatitis B vaccine and reassess in 1 month
D. Start ribavirin to prevent flare
E. Monitor ALT weekly and start antivirals only if ALT rises above 200
POST.r: HBsAg positivity confirms chronic HBV, and high-dose prolonged steroids can precipitate severe reactivation. The analytical step is recognizing that waiting for HBV DNA results delays necessary prophylaxis when the trigger (high-dose steroids) is imminent. A high-barrier antiviral should be started concurrently. Vaccination cannot prevent reactivation in established chronic HBV.

POST.st: A 76-year-old woman with diffuse atherosclerosis presents with sudden severe abdominal pain. Exam shows marked pain with minimal tenderness. BP 92/54 mmHg, HR 118/min. Creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL (baseline unknown). Lactate is 3.8 mmol/L. The team hesitates to order contrast imaging because of the kidney injury. What is the best next step?
o: A. Obtain noncontrast CT first to avoid contrast nephropathy
B. Obtain CT angiography with IV contrast immediately while resuscitating
C. Start TPN and observe overnight
D. Treat empirically for pancreatitis
E. Obtain colonoscopy for ischemic colitis
POST.r: The analytical challenge is weighing contrast nephropathy risk against the life-threatening nature of acute mesenteric ischemia. CTA should not be delayed even with AKI when clinical suspicion is high — missed AMI is rapidly fatal, while contrast-associated nephropathy is manageable. Noncontrast CT and colonoscopy miss actionable arterial findings. Simultaneous resuscitation is essential.

POST.st: A 57-year-old woman with a history of post-ERCP pancreatitis is admitted for RUQ pain. She is afebrile with stable vitals. Labs show AST 210 U/L, ALT 260 U/L, ALP 190 U/L, bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones and CBD diameter of 7 mm without a visible stone. What is the best approach?
o: A. Proceed directly to ERCP tonight
B. Obtain MRCP or EUS to confirm choledocholithiasis before ERCP
C. Give antibiotics and plan cholecystectomy only
D. Start heparin for hepatic vein thrombosis
E. Start TPA for biliary obstruction
POST.r: This is intermediate-risk choledocholithiasis (abnormal LFTs, mildly dilated CBD, no high-risk criteria like cholangitis or bilirubin >4 mg/dL). Noninvasive confirmation with MRCP or EUS is preferred before ERCP, especially given her prior post-ERCP pancreatitis. The analytical key is appropriate risk stratification to avoid unnecessary ERCP and its complications.

POST.st: A 40-year-old woman is hospitalized for an asthma exacerbation. She has no GI symptoms but reports her father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 52. She has never been screened. What is the most appropriate screening plan?
o: A. Begin screening at age 45 with annual FIT
B. Begin screening now with colonoscopy and repeat every 10 years
C. Begin screening now with colonoscopy and repeat every 5 years if normal
D. Begin screening at age 50 with colonoscopy every 10 years
E. No screening needed because she is asymptomatic
POST.r: With a first-degree relative diagnosed with CRC before age 60, screening should begin at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest affected relative's diagnosis (whichever is earlier), using colonoscopy with 5-year intervals. The analytical pitfall is applying average-risk guidelines (starting at 45 with 10-year intervals) to someone who qualifies for high-risk screening due to family history.

POST.st: A 72-year-old woman with septic shock is in the ICU on norepinephrine at 0.25 µg/kg/min with rising lactate and cool extremities. She has been NPO for 2 days. An order is placed to start continuous enteral feeds overnight. Her abdomen is soft but mildly distended. What is the best next step?
o: A. Start full-rate gastric feeds now to prevent mucosal atrophy
B. Start trophic feeds and advance rapidly every 2 hours
C. Hold enteral feeds until adequately resuscitated and vasopressor requirements are stable or decreasing
D. Switch to bolus feeds to improve tolerance
E. Place a postpyloric tube and start full-rate feeds despite shock
POST.r: The analytical challenge is recognizing that enteral feeding during active shock with escalating vasopressors and rising lactate risks bowel ischemia. Guidelines recommend holding EN until the patient is adequately resuscitated and vasopressor requirements are stable or de-escalating. The pitfall is assuming 'some feeds are always safe' — even trophic feeding requires hemodynamic stability.
